title: Projected Cooling Degree Days U.S. (RCP4.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDD is often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Projected Cumulative Precipitation (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset shows the change in annual average total precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the total precipitation in 2000 is actually an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Precipitation changes are projected to be more varied across the world, generally showing increases in mean precipitation in high-latitude regions and a pole-ward shift of subtropical arid regions. In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. Except in the few areas that are projected to see substantial drying, historically extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. Even as precipitation increases, dry periods are projected to increase in length and frequency. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The cumulative precipitation for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by adding all daily precipitation data over a given year. The cumulative precipitations were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in cumulative precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that cumulative precipitation is decreasing.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the cumulative precipitation in 2000 was calculated as an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Road Traffic Death Rates
description:
The traffic deaths rate data produced by the World Health Organization (WHO) give mortality data from road traffic injuries. To estimate road traffic fatal injury, countries were classified into 4 groups as follows: (1) Countries with death registration data completeness of at least 80%. For this category, one of the following data points was used: death registration, projection of the most recent death registration, reported death, or projected reported deaths. (2) Countries with other sources of information on cause of death. This group includes India, Iran, Thailand, and Vietnam. For these countries, a regression method was used to project forward the most recent year for which an estimate of total road traffic deaths was available. (3) Countries with population less than 150,000 and without eligible death registration data. For these countries, the deaths reported in the survey were used directly, without adjustment. (4) Countries without eligible death registration data. For these countries, a negative binomial regression model was used. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

description:
The Ecoregions Prioritized for Conservation released by The Nature Conservancy (TNC) provides a vision for conservation success for ecological systems, natural communities, and species representative of an ecoregion by showing the boundaries of areas that TNC has prioritized for conservation in 2011. Many portfolio areas were derived from ecoregional assessments, but other priorities derived using other planning methodologies are included in this global data set. Ecoregional assessment is a method for setting geographic priorities based on the status of biodiversity, habitat condition, threats, and sociopolitical conditions in an ecoregion. In more detail, ecoregional assessments use ecoregions as the unit of analysis.   
  
For an ecoregion or collection of ecoregions, TNC develops and disseminates finer-scale data on the distribution and status of biodiversity, habitat condition, current and future threats, and the sociopolitical conditions that influence conservation success within those ecoregions. These finer-scale data allow TNC to set long-term conservation goals for ecosystems, natural communities, and imperiled or declining species representative of an ecoregion, and to establish ecoregional priorities for resource allocation—specific landscapes, threats to biodiversity, and strategic opportunities that affect one or more ecoregions and demand immediate attention. Ecoregional data also provide a baseline against which TNC can measure progress toward the long-term goals for the representative ecosystems and species within an ecoregion. [Archived] Cumulative Climate Impacts on Marine Ecosystems
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](85a08a4d-9336-4d18-9aaa-b7cb97bc6abf) as a replacement.**_
  
This cumulative impact index ranging from ranging from 0 (no change) to 1 (maximum change) for the impact of climate change on oceans was calculated using sea surface temperature (SST), ocean productivity measured by chlorophyll (CHL), and ocean circulation by Ramirez et al. (2017). The data to calculate were from the longest time series of remote-sensing records (annual composites) on SST (1980-2014), CHL (1979-2014), and marine currents (1980-2014) available to provide finest-scale measurements of the impacts of climate change on the marine environment globally.   
  
Pixel basis, least-squares linear regression of annual information from SST, CHL, and the eastern and northern components of water speed were used for deriving the significance of temporal trends and its magnitudes (slopes; that is, annual changes in target features) over the past 3 decades. CHL data were sourced online as annual composites, whereas data on SST and marine currents were obtained on a monthly basis and averaged yearly to generate a linear relationship to extract slopes. This calculation was repeated for every pixel of the globe. These magnitudes were combined to obtain the spatially explicit Cumulative Impact Index.   
  
Different layers were first resampled following a bilinear interpolation procedure to match the spatial resolution of the coarsest SST product (that is, 1° grid). Absolute values for the slopes of obtained trends (a proxy to the magnitude of environmental changes) were then standardized to the maximum value to make all variables comparable. These relative values were subsequently added on a pixel basis and standardized again to the maximum value. In this way, researchers obtained a dimensionless index ranging from 0 (no change) to 1 (maximum change), thereby providing information about spatial heterogeneity in the magnitude of environmental changes and highlighting those marine areas that have undergone the largest changes in their environmental conditions. Projected Frost Free Season (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Average High Temperature
description:
Annual average high temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature
description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average minimum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the minimum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average minimum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in annual average minimum temperature is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual average minimum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily minimum temperature data over a given year. The average annual minimum temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average minimum temperature.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual minimum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.  
  
### Additional Information

Seychelles Storm Surge and Sea Level Rise Exposure
description: This dataset was developed in 2019 by a team of researchers at the University of Michigan. The map shows the geographic distribution of an index developed to represent the exposure of Mahé’s coastline to the impacts of a storm surge event. Due to the minimal record of storm surge data in Seychelles, the difficulty of gauging how global climate change could increase the probability of a storm surge occurring, and the fact that data parameters typically used in storm surge prediction models weren’t made available to the research team, this data set identifies the regions that would be most exposed to the impacts of a storm surge, rather than the likelihood of a storm surge occurring. Considering these existing constraints, this model is processes-based and not calibrated by existing storm surge data; therefore, it is purely theoretical. The data was created in ArcGIS using a multi-criteria analysis model with elevation, slope, topographic wetness index, cost distance from river, soil type, and vegetation cover as criteria of interest. These variables were scaled, weighted, arranged into a pairwise comparison matrix, assigned relative importance, put into an Analytic Hierarchy Process program to calculate weighted sums, and ultimately produce a storm surge exposure index. A more comprehensive explanation of how this index was created can be found in the report linked below.

title: Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Station Forecasts
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Station Forecasts dataset provides air quality forecasts for a group of cities taking part in the [CityAQ project](https://airquality.gsfc.nasa.gov/cityaq-pilot-combine-local-monitoring-data-geos-cf-model-outputs-develop-city-scale-operational). Ozone (O₃) concentrations are forecasted at the station level, and are shown in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). The dataset is updated daily and shows the forecasted concentration of O₃ for the following five days. The forecast is generated by the source at an hourly time step, and Resource Watch aggregates to the maximum 8-hour concentration.
  
  
Ground-level ozone is an air pollutant that is harmful to breathe and damages crops and other vegetation. Unlike stratospheric ozone in the upper atmosphere, which protects us from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays and forms naturally, ground-level ozone forms when emissions of volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides react in the presence of heat and sunlight. Gasoline-burning vehicles are large sources of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Other sources include consumer products such as paints, insecticides, cleaners, as well as industrial solvents and chemical manufacturing. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)](https://www.epa.gov/ground-level-ozone-pollution/health-effects-ozone-pollution), ozone irritates respiratory systems, can aggravate asthma, and can damage cells that line your lungs. Ozone may also aggravate chronic lung diseases such as emphysema and bronchitis and may cause permanent lung damage. These effects can be worse in children and exercising adults.
The CityAQ project aims to help cities around the world to know more about the levels, sources, and impacts of air pollution. Many of the places with the highest level of pollution have the least information to work with to know their air quality and manage it accordingly. Free and publicly-available air quality data from satellites, along with low-cost sensor systems and output from air quality models, have the potential to augment high-quality, regulatory-grade data in countries with in situ monitoring networks and provide much needed air quality information in countries without them. By combining the strengths of these multiple monitoring technologies, an integrated air pollution network has the potential to provide free/low cost and publicly-accessible air quality information to health and air quality managers in cities around the world.

  
  
These forecasts were modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) by combining local air quality monitoring information, made available with support from the World Resources Institute (WRI), with the outputs of NASA’s global Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). The CityAQ project objective is to provide participating cities with useful forecasts that they can use to anticipate air quality events, communicate with stakeholders, and manage local interventions more effectively. It looks to test and refine a methodology for combining locally held information with globally consistent analysis to offer new local tools and, in the future, potentially improve global analysis by aggregating fragmented local data into programmatically useful datasets and make the GEOS-CF forecasts usable by all world cities. The organizations involved in the CityAQ project aim to refine a scalable approach for engaging with users to co-create air quality tools that leverage and extend existing scientific analysis.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Validated or raw station level measurement data is collected from either government sites or [OpenAQ](https://openaq.org/#/).
Validated air quality observations of government sites were obtained from the air quality data portals of [Bogotá](http://rmcab.ambientebogota.gov.co/home/map) and [Sao Paulo](https://servicos.cetesb.sp.gov.br/qa/), or in the case of the Mexican cities of Monterrey, Guadalajara, Salamanca and León were shared directly by state governments. Near-real time, raw observations for the cities of Addis, Jakarta, as well as the following cities in the mexican state of Guanajuato: Guanajuato city, Irapuato, San Miguel de Allende, Silao, Celaya, San Luis de la Paz and Abasolo were retrieved from OpenAQ. For station-level data to be included in OpenAQ’s catalogue, it must meet the minimum data requirements as described by [OpenAQ](https://github.com/openaq/openaq-fetch/blob/master/README.md).  
 
   
  
Meteorological and atmospheric chemistry information at each of the CityAQ stations is obtained from NASA’s GEOS-CF model. GEOS-CF provides global hourly analyses and forecasts of atmospheric composition at 25-kilometer spatial resolution. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. Any correlation between cloud cover and surface PM2.5 should be captured similarly by GCC and GOCART. The PM2.5 dataset shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GCC module. A detailed description of GEOS-CF can be found in [Keller et al. (2021)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1029/2020MS002413). 
 
  
  
Since the model output is too coarse to resolve fine-scale air quality features characteristic of urban environments, a bias-correction algorithm is applied to account for the spatial representation error, as well as other potential model biases such as errors in the model representation of transport or chemistry.  The bias-correction methodology uses the [XGBoost machine learning algorithm](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#) to develop a machine learning model that predicts the model bias at each of the observation stations as a function of the current meteorological and chemical environment and time. Once trained, the machine learning model is used on a daily basis to calculate the expected model bias at a given site and this value is added to the ‘raw’ (i.e., uncorrected) GEOS-CF predictions.
 
  
  
The machine learning training is based on the 2018–2019 observation–model differences and designed to predict the systematic model bias between hourly PM2.5 observations and the model predictions at that location. These biases can be due to errors in the model, such as emission estimates, sub-grid-scale local influences or meteorology and chemistry. Since model biases are often site-specific, a separate machine learning model is used for each site. The input features to the machine learning algorithm encompass 9 meteorological parameters (as simulated by the GEOS-CF model: surface northward and eastward wind components, surface temperature and skin temperature, surface relative humidity, total cloud coverage, total precipitation, surface pressure, and planetary boundary layer height) and the modeled surface concentrations of 51 chemical species (O3, NOx, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and aerosols). In addition, it provides as input features the hour-of-day, day of week, and month of the year; these allow the machine learning model to identify systematic observation-model mismatches related to the diurnal, weekly and seasonal cycle of the pollutants. This bias correction methodology is based on [Keller et al. (2021)](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/21/3555/2021/).

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows CityAQ datasets for fine particulate matter [(PM2.5)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/f5599d62-7f3d-41c7-b3fd-9f8e08ee7b2a) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/8ee6a93b-ab7a-41a8-95f5-3d684626d9ea).

City Expansion Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The city expansion index dataset shows outward and upward urban growth in 377 cities globally that have a population of over 1 million residents. Outward growth is the horizontal expansion of buildings and upward growth is the vertical expansion of buildings. The final dataset was normalized into comparable values called the Upward Growth Index and Outward Growth Index. A higher expansion index value means more growth is occurring. The dataset uses remote sensing data collected between 2000 and 2014.

  
  
This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) as part of the World Resources Report (WRR) Towards a More Equal City. It is intended to highlight regional trends in urban expansion and differences in urban structure within and between cities. Ultimately, it can be used to help governments understand how urban expansion can be managed in a way that achieves more equitable access to core services for the under-served while bringing wider economic and environmental benefits to cities. For the dataset to paint a complete picture it should ideally be used in conjunction with a matching dataset on the socioeconomic information of the city.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was created using a combination of remote sensing data to determine upward and outward expansion in cities with a metropolitan population greater than 1 million. Remote sensing data was collected from mean summer backscatter power ratio (PR) from NASA's SeaWinds microwave scatterometer (Ku-band, 13.4 GHz) and built-up area from the multitemporal Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL). The data showed the outward growth of urban built-up areas between 2000 and 2014 measured from the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) and upward growth between 2001 and 2009 measured using the power ratio (PR) from NASA’s SeaWinds microwave scatterometer. Each dataset was reprocessed to have the same spatial resolution of 0.05 degrees (about 5.6 km at the equator). To determine which cities had a metropolitan population greater than 1 million, Landscan data created by the Oak Ridge National Laboratory was combined with the Oxford Economics database to create a combined dataset of 377 cities. 
  
  
 Researchers overlayed an 11x11 pixel grid (121 total pixels) over each city using the dataset Populated Places from Natural Earth to create a unified boundary to measure the cities growth. The 11x11 grids were extracted and all grid cells with a built up value less than 20 percent were masked in GHSL. Total upward and outward growth were then calculated using the remaining pixels for each city by using a cluster analysis to group each pixel into similar urban growth patterns and structures. Finally, the values were converted into the upward urban growth index and outward urban growth index to allow for comparison of the values across cities. 
  
  
The final dataset was presented in raster format at a spatial resolution of 0.28 degrees (20.98 square kilometers at the equator). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.
description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDD is often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4c6ba704-12f3-4954-92af-6c248c584233), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/09e43293-98f1-4618-8e7e-d9f72cd5a4d7), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22).   
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original LOCA dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Historical Imagery
description:
### Overview  
  
The Historical Imagery dataset is a compilation of high quality Landsat imagery for each year from 2013-2016. These images show a detailed picture of the landscape at the Earth’s surface, e.g., forests, ice, freshwater, grasslands, desert and urban areas. Landsat data was collected continuously by satellite sensors. These sensors collected approximately 22 complete pictures of the Earth per year, with a spatial resolution of 30 meters (m). The satellite imagery was processed with Google Earth Engine’s Simple Composite algorithm. This algorithm converts the images to [top of atmosphere (TOA) reflectance](https://un-spider.org/node/10958) values and removes cloud-covered pixels.

  
  
Understanding the Earth’s changing landscape is critical to many environmental issues: agriculture, water usage, forest coverage and natural disasters. In agriculture, Landsat data can be used to predict crop production, help farmers make planting decisions and settle water usage disputes. Landsat imagery shows changes in forest coverage, which is crucial to forest management and protection. Forest coverage influences the environment in many ways, including carbon storage and flood control. Landsat imagery is also a valuable tool for analyzing natural disasters such as floods, fires, droughts and volcanic eruptions. In areas affected by natural disasters, before and after imagery can be used to map damage, plan recovery efforts, and assess future risk.

  
  
The Historical Imagery dataset was generated by [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/). Earth Engine is a tool for visualizing and analyzing geospatial datasets. The platform hosts satellite imagery in a public data archive for academic, non-profit, business and government users. In addition to hosting data, Earth Engine provides a variety of algorithms and processed datasets, including climate, surface temperature, weather and land cover. Earth Engine is part of Google’s overall mission to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible. The satellite data used to generate the Historical Imagery dataset was provided by [Landsat](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/nli/landsat). Landsat is a joint effort between the [United States Geological Survey (USGS)](https://www.usgs.gov/) and the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/). Founded in 1972, Landsat manages satellites that continuously acquire images of the Earth. Landsat’s mission is to provide uninterrupted data and imagery of the Earth to help with decision-making about natural resources and the environment.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Historical Imagery dataset was generated from images of the Earth collected by instruments aboard the [Landsat satellites](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/nli/landsat/landsat-satellite-missions?qt-science_support_page_related_con=0#qt-science_support_page_related_con). These satellites crossed every point on Earth once every 16 days and each provided 22 complete pictures of the Earth each year. Each pixel in these images has a resolution of 30 m.

  
  
The satellite imagery was processed using [Google Earth Engine’s Simple Composite algorithm](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/apidocs/ee-algorithms-landsat-simplecomposite). This algorithm selected a subset of pixels at each location and converted them to top of atmosphere (TOA) reflectance. This conversion is a linear transformation used to correct satellite data for variations in solar angle and the scattering of light that occurs as light travels through the atmosphere and reflects off the Earth. The simple cloud score was used to find the images with the least cloud cover. This algorithm scored TOA data pixels by their relative cloudiness from 0 (least cloudy) to 100 (most cloudy). After the pixels were scored, the median of the least cloudy pixels were used, thus selecting the least cloudy images. These images were used to generate the Historical Imagery composites. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data

description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows boats detected using satellite data collected by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instrument. VIIRS only detects the activity of lit boats. The data shows patterns of vessel activity and can provide indications of fishing activity within marine protected areas (MPAs) and across exclusive economic zone (EEZ) boundaries. Generally, EEZs are defined as the area within 200 nautical miles of a country’s coastline.   
  
The dataset is published by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (NOAA) and the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). The dataset has global spatial coverage, gives point location (latitude and longitude) of boat detections. The data collection began in 2017 and is updated daily.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Lit fishing boat features detected by the VIIRS day/night band (DNB) data show up as spikes of light. A set of algorithms has been developed for automatic detection of spikes and characterization of the sharpness of spike features.   
  
A spike detection algorithm generates a list of candidate boat detections. A second algorithm measures the height of the spikes for the discard of ionospheric energetic particle detections and to rate boat detections as either strong or weak. A sharpness index is used to label boat detections that appear blurry due to the scattering of light by clouds. The candidate spikes are then compared with a separate VIIRS gas flares data set to identify detections that were also found to be gas flares.   
  
Based on the sharpness index, scan properties, and the gas flare indication, each candidate spike is assigned a quality flag that separates the detections into boats, blurry detections, and gas flares. Based on the location of the boat detections, they are also assigned information such as whether it is in an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) or a marine protected area (MPA). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/7/3/3020).

Tree Cover Gain
description:
### Overview  
  
The Tree Cover Gain dataset measures areas of tree cover gain from 2001 through 2012. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Gain is mapped for all areas that did not have tree cover in 2000 and had ≥ 50% cover in 2012. Longer-lived regrowing stands of tree cover that did not begin as non-forest within the study period were not mapped as forest gain. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 1 arc second which is approximately 30 m × 30 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.
  
  
Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species and supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is playing an incredibly important role since it [absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the gain in tree cover of global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity.


  
  
The dataset has been created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. 

  
  
### Methodology  
  
The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2019 interval. 

  
  
The following steps were taken to pre-process the images:
  
  
1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed.
  
  
2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water.
  
  
3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another.

  
  
Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover gain. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows the [Tree Cover](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/027799db-c161-462a-9c20-aeb97b84e06e) and the [Tree Cover Loss](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5c5e654e-182b-4ab4-8a3c-edff79cc68ea) from the same dataset.

description:
Increases in the rates of hospital admission for heat stress are one potential impact of rising global temperatures. Tracking Crude Rate of Hospitalization for Heat Stress per 100,000 Population can help document changes over place and time, monitor vulnerable areas, and evaluate the results of local climate-adaptation strategies. 

Heat stress can manifest in a number of clinical outcomes, and people with chronic health problems (e.g., cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity) are more susceptible to the effects of heat than healthy individuals. For these reasons, heat stress may not be listed as the primary diagnosis. This indicator therefore includes all cases where heat stress is explicitly listed as the primary diagnosis or any other diagnosis. The hospital data shown here are provided by state and/or local public health departments to the National Environmental Public Health Tracking Program. Data are based on the date of admission rather than the date of discharge. For these measures, admission date is limited to between May 1 and September 30 for each year. These data represent number of admissions rather than number of individuals admitted to the hospital.  The Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Tracking Network suppresses data for counties with non-zero counts less than 6 and population less than 100,000 to protect confidentiality. This data set covers the United States from 2000 to 2016. 

Data on states designated as 'unstable', or counties corresponding with relative standard error greater than 30%, have been excluded in this visualization. See the original data source for this information.

description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows renewable energy consumption in 259 countries from 1990 to present. In this dataset, renewable energy sources are defined as hydropower, solid and liquid biofuels, wind, solar, biogas, geothermal, marine, and waste to energy. 

  
  
The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative, and the data was compiled by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations Statistics Divisions (UNSD). IEA and UNDC are the primary developers of internationally comparable national energy statistics. This dataset tracks the progress of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 7.2, to advance the target of increase substantially the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. 

  
  
Resource Watch also shows [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database.  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was compiled using data from the International Energy Agency (IEA) energy statistics, complemented by the United Nations (UN) database when IEA data was not available. IEA data contained the most comprehensive and accurate data for countries that were a part of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), as well as 75 non-OECD countries. In the case of smaller non-OECD countries, extrapolations of country data provided by the UN Statistics Division were used. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.seforall.org/sites/default/files/l/2013/09/9-gtf_ch4.pdf).

title: [Archived] Global Hunger Index
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c37b0b21-3d11-46ea-ba5d-4be4c0caa8ae) as a replacement.**_
  
### Overview  
  
The Global Hunger Indices show the state of hunger worldwide in 2018, along with three reference years in 2000, 2005, and 2010. The indices capture the multidimensional nature of hunger by calculating Global Hunger Index (GHI) scores comprised of four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality.  
  
The 2018 Global Hunger Index is published jointly by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe to measure and track hunger and to spotlight areas with the greatest need to eliminate hunger. The GHI scores are calculated on a 0-100 scale, where 0 indicates no hunger and 100 demonstrates complete hunger. A high GHI score, broadly speaking, can indicate a lack of food, a low-quality diet, insufficient child caregiving practices, an unhealthy environment, or all of these factors. In the GHI by Severity layers, countries are classified as having low, moderate, serious, alarming, or extremely alarming scales of hunger.   
  
### Methodology  
  
GHI scores were calculated using a three-step process that draws on available data from various sources to capture the multidimensional nature of hunger.  
  
First, for each country, values were determined for four indicators:  
  
1. Undernourishment: the share of the population that is undernourished (that is, whose caloric intake is insufficient);  
  
2. Child wasting: the share of children under the age of five who are wasted (that is, who have low weight for their height, reflecting acute undernutrition);  
  
3. Child stunting: the share of children under the age of five who are stunted (that is, who have low height for their age, reflecting chronic undernutrition); and  
  
4. Child Mortality: the mortality rate of children under the age of five (in part, a reflection of the fatal mix of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments).  
  

Second, each of the four component indicators was given a standardized score on a 100-point scale based on the highest observed level for the indicator on a global scale in recent decades.  
  
Third, standardized scores were aggregated to calculate the GHI score for each country, with each of the three dimensions (inadequate food supply, child mortality, and child undernutrition, which is composed equally of child stunting and child wasting) given equal weight.  
  
This three-step process results in GHI scores on a 100-point GHI Severity Scale, where 0 is the best score (no hunger) and 100 is the worst. In practice, neither of these extremes is reached. A value of 0 would mean that a country had no undernourished people in the population, no children younger than five who were wasted or stunted, and no children who died before their fifth birthday. A value of 100 would signify that a country’s undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality levels were each at approximately the highest levels observed worldwide in recent decades. The GHI Severity Scale shows the severity of hunger - from low to extremely alarming - associated with the range of possible GHI scores.

description:
The Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI) supported the development of the Global-Aridity Database. This database is designed for use in models of sustainable development, biodiversity and environmental conservation, poverty alleviation, and adaption to climate change globally, in particular in developing countries, and provides data for each month between 1970 and 2000 at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds. This data set is the aridity index (AI), which is calculated as the ratio of mean annual precipitation to mean annual potential evapotranspiration (PET), using data from the WorldClim Global Climate Database. The yearly precipitation values are available directly from the WorldClim database, and the PET values are derived from a selection of WorldClim variables. PET is a measure of the rate at which water evaporates from the Earth's surface into the atmosphere. It is influenced by several factors, including solar radiation, temperature, air humidity, and wind speed. Other contributing factors include the leaf area index of an area, as water pooling on top of leaves and tree canopies can lead to faster evaporation than if precipitating water entered the soil layer. title: Groundwater Vulnerability to Floods and Droughts
description:
The German Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources (BGR) partnered with UNESCO's International Hydrological Programme and the International Association of Hydrogeologists to coordinate the World-wide Hydrogeological Mapping and Assessment Programme (WHYMAP). The Map of Global Groundwater Vulnerability (GWV) to Floods and Droughts at the scale of 1:25,000,000 is a WHYMAP product that rates groundwater systems on a scale of 1 to 7 according to their vulnerability to drought and flood events. Vulnerability is defined as a system's sensitivity to natural and/or human impacts, and the ability of the system to cope with these impacts. This information can be used to prioritize which groundwater resources can be relied on in case of a natural disaster.

The maps of groundwater systems were sourced from national, regional, and global sources. Many aquifer boundaries were sourced from the WHYMAP Groundwater Resources Map (GRM). The GRM includes major groundwater basins, areas with complex hydrogeological structures, and local and shallow aquifers. These were complemented by aquifers in fluvial deposits of large rivers from the Geological Map of the World, aquifers in carbonate rocks—usually karstified—from the World Map of Carbonate Rock Outcrops, and the WHYMAP database for aquifers with nonrenewable groundwater. The extent of the impact of different natural disasters on aquifers and their groundwater resources differs depending on factors such as the origin of the disaster, its intensity and frequency, the hydrogeological conditions and geographical position of the aquifer (coastal area or a floodplain), and other factors affecting vulnerability (shallow or deep, whether groundwater is nonrenewable). The GWV uses a simplified version of the DRASTIC index for assessing groundwater vulnerability, measuring aquifer vulnerability according to the type of aquifer and the aquifer’s groundwater recharge rate. Aquifer types are assessed according to the map sources mentioned above. Groundwater recharge rates are calculated using the WaterGAP hydrogeological model and categorized as < 20 mm/year, 20-100 mm/year, or > 100 mm/year. 

A total vulnerability range (TVR) is assigned to each aquifer based on its type and recharge rate. Aquifer type is weighted more than rate of recharge in this calculation, since aquifers in carbonate rocks (often karstified) or in fluvial deposits of large rivers and shallow and local aquifers are all highly vulnerable to natural disasters—particularly floods, storms, and tsunamis—and are also highly vulnerable to droughts in arid and semiarid regions. Natural disasters include 1) hydro-climatic events (floods, droughts, storms); 2) geological events (earthquakes, volcanic activity); and 3) events caused by a combination of hydroclimatic and geological factors (tsunamis, landslides). The GWV focuses on hydroclimatic events, and the vulnerability of each aquifer is assessed for floods and droughts. The map assigns 7 categories of vulnerability based on the combination of flood and drought vulnerability (low, low; low, moderate; etc). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: nat.1 Burned areas (modis)
Fully and Highly Protected Marine Areas
description:
### Overview  
  
The Fully and Highly Protected Marine Areas dataset as shown on Resource Watch presents marine protected areas (MPAs) that are fully or highly protected. The [Marine Protection Atlas (MPAtlas)](https://mpatlas.org/) uses the [World Database on Protected Areas](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/thematic-areas/marine-protected-areas) as a starting point, then assesses the current protection status of listed MPAs based on additional sources and research. This global dataset was first created in 2020 and in the future will be regularly updated, as new MPAs are created, protections change, and currently designated areas are implemented.

  
  
MPAs are essential for safeguarding biodiversity and the health of marine ecosystems. They provide sanctuary for species to mature and reproduce, and they help restore healthy populations within and beyond their borders. MPAs also build resilience against threats such as climate change and pollution by maintaining vital natural processes, storing carbon, buffering coastlines, and ensuring sustainable food supplies for coastal communities. However, different MPAs may offer different levels of protection, from minor restrictions to the full exclusion of most commercial activity. Robust scientific evidence indicates that no-take zones (where no extractive activities are allowed) and highly protected areas yield the greatest conservation benefits.

  
  
The MPAtlas brings together the best available information on marine protection around the world, so that the marine conservation community can work together to protect at least [30% of the world's oceans by 2030](https://www.campaignfornature.org/science-page). This more detailed approach to MPA data provides a more nuanced look at progress toward conservation goals and the outcomes that can be expected from existing protections.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
MPAtlas takes the WDPA as its starting point and examines the listed MPAs in depth, adding to or replacing WDPA records with information from original research using more detailed or up-to-date sources, such as national or regional databases, official documentation, or management plans. These additions can include more accurate spatial data, such as the addition of boundaries for individual zones within an MPA. It can also include more detailed information about site regulations and management, both of which are directly related to conservation outcomes.

  
  
MPAtlas coverage numbers differ from those of other sources for two primary reasons:
1. MPAtlas attempts to identify and distinguish protected areas that are legally designated but are still awaiting implementation from those that are fully in effect on the water. The project also identifies committed or proposed protected areas that have not yet achieved legal or authoritative recognition.
2. MPA coverage data is reported by protection level, as no-take and fully and highly protected areas are those which afford the greatest conservation benefits. The project accomplishes this by conducting detailed assessments using widely-accepted, scientifically-based criteria for measuring an MPA’s protection level and associated conservation outcomes. Detailed information about the assessment process [can be found here](https://marine-conservation.org/mpatlas-assessments/).

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://mpatlas.org/methods).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [the full WDPA](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio007-World-Database-on-Protected-Areas_replacement) and [the MPA subset](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio007b-Marine-Protected-Areas), on which the MPAtlas is based.

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the Marine Protected Atlas. The MPAtlas includes all MPAs in the WDPA, but because these are already mapped elsewhere, Resource Watch displays only those MPAtlas entries with confirmed partial or complete protections from fishing and extractive commercial activity.

title: Soil carbon density (LM v3)
Landslide Hazard Alerts
description:
The global Landslide Hazard Assessment for Situational Awareness (LHASA) model is developed by NASA to provide situational awareness of landslide hazards for a wide range of users. Precipitation is a common trigger of landslides. The Integrated Multisatellite Retrievals for the Global Precipitation Measurement mission (IMERG) data shows recent precipitation, updated every 30 minutes. A LHASA landslide “nowcast” is created by comparing GPM data from the last 7 days to the long-term precipitation record provided by the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) Multisatellite Precipitation Analysis (TMPA). Because IMERG data are only available starting in 2014, the record of historical rainfall was established by the TMPA, comparing 2001 to the present. The TMPA rainfall probability distributions were then compared to those of IMERG, and the rainfall thresholds were adjusted so that the IMERG data more closely mapped to those of the TMPA archive. The past 7 days of rainfall are considered, with each day weighted according to its date before present, with the last 24 hours having the most impact. In places where precipitation is unusually high, the susceptibility of the terrain is evaluated based on the global landslide susceptibility map, which includes quantitative information on whether (1) roads have been built, (2) trees have been cut down or burned, (3) a major tectonic fault is nearby, (4) the local bedrock is weak, or (5) the hillsides are steep. title: Biodiversity Hotspots
description:
### Overview  
  
Biodiversity hotspots, a classification system created by the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF), include some of our planet’s most biologically diverse yet threatened terrestrial areas. An area is qualified as a hotspot if it contains at least 1,500 species of vascular plants found nowhere else on Earth (known as “endemic” species) and it has lost at least 70 percent of its primary native vegetation. Between 1988 and 2016, 36 biodiversity hotspots have been identified globally.   
  
### Methodology  
  
Hotspots were defined by Norman Myers in 1988 when he published a seminal paper identifying 10 tropical forest “hotspots.” These regions were characterized both by exceptional levels of plant endemism, meaning plants found nowhere else on Earth, and serious levels of habitat loss. Conservation International (CI) adopted Myers’s hotspots as its institutional blueprint in 1989. In 1999, CI undertook a global review, which introduced quantitative thresholds for the designation of biodiversity hotspots and resulted in the identification of 25. 

  
  
In 2005, an additional analysis brought the total number of biodiversity hotspots to 34, based on the work of nearly 400 specialists. In 2011, the Forests of East Australia were identified as the 35th hotspot by a team of researchers from the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization working with CI. In February 2016, the North American Coastal Plain was recognized as meeting the criteria and became the world’s 36th hotspot. Potential Natural Vegetation
description:
Potential Natural Vegetation is a data set created by EarthStat to identify what vegetation would be most likely to exist now in the absence of human activities. In regions not dominated by human land use, the vegetation types are those currently observed from a satellite. This differs from presettlement natural vegetation to the extent that vegetation types have changed because of changing environmental conditions such as climate and CO₂ concentrations. 1 km resolution DISCover data were classified under the Olson Global Ecosystems (OGE) framework to derive the potential vegetation data set. First the 94 OGE classes were reclassified into 15 potential vegetation types and 3 additional classes: land use, wetlands, and water. Wetlands are poorly characterized in the DISCover data and were thus ignored; only upland natural vegetation was considered. Each 5 minute resolution grid cell was searched among the 1 km pixels for the dominant potential upland vegetation class and was assigned to be the potential vegetation. Some grid cells had 2 dominant potential vegetation classes, or none. In these cases, the search was iterated to the adjacent 1 km pixels until a dominant potential vegetation class was found.
