title: Projected Sea Level Rise
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows projected sea surface height around the world for every year through 2100, relative to average sea surface height during 1986–2005. Sea surface height (SSH) varies geographically: shifting surface winds, the expansion of warming ocean water, and the addition of melting ice can alter ocean currents which, in turn, lead to changes in sea level that vary from place to place. Past and present variations in the distribution of land ice affect the shape and gravitational field of the Earth, which also cause regional fluctuations in sea level. Additional variations in sea level are caused by the influence of more localized processes such as sediment compaction and tectonics. To properly reflect this variability, the projections comprise a time series of 1° resolution geospatial grids.

  
  
Over relatively short time spans (hours to years), the influence of tides, storms, and climatic variability—such as El Niño—dominates sea level variations. Earthquakes and landslides can also have an effect by causing changes in land height and, sometimes, tsunamis. Over longer time spans (decades to centuries), the influence of climate change—with consequent changes in volume of ocean water and land ice—is the main contributor to sea level change in most regions. Ocean thermal expansion and glacier melting were the dominant contributors to 20th century global mean sea level rise. It is very likely that the rate of sea level rise during the 21st century will exceed the rate observed during 1971–2010.

  
  
These data were used in the construction of figures for the Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the United Nations body for assessing the science related to climate change. As the IPCC states, "Continued emission of greenhouse gases will cause further warming and long-lasting changes in all components of the climate system, increasing the likelihood of severe, pervasive and irreversible impacts for people and ecosystems." Over recent decades, more than 90% of the net energy increase of the climate system has been stored in the ocean, and its warming provides both strong evidence for and measurement of a changing climate. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The final projections for global mean sea level rise represent the sum of anticipated contributions from a number of different sources. These include: ocean heat uptake and the subsequent thermal expansion of seawater; land water storage and changes in land surface characteristics that influence runoff or evapotranspiration rates, such as dams, irrigation schemes, or groundwater depletion; diminishing glaciers; and changes in the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, including direct outflows of water from melting and icebergs as well as more complex interactions between the sheets, the land surface on which they rest, and the ocean.

  
  
Annual time series for change in global mean surface air temperature and global mean sea level rise due to thermal expansion in the past and during the 21st century under different emissions scenarios were obtained from a set of 21 Atmosphere–Ocean General Circulation Models (AOGCMs) of the [Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5)](https://pcmdi.llnl.gov/mips/cmip5/). AOGCMs have components representing the ocean, atmosphere, land, and cryosphere, and simulate sea surface height changes resulting from volcanic eruptions and changes in solar irradiance, and from anthropogenic increases in GHGs and aerosols. AOGCMs also exhibit internally generated climate variability, including such patterns as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and others that affect sea level. As in the real world, ocean density, circulation and sea level are dynamically connected in AOGCMs and evolve together. 

  
  
The overall contribution of an ice mass to sea level involves changes to either its surface mass balance (SMB) or changes in the dynamics of ice flow that affect outflow (i.e., solid ice discharge) to the ocean. SMB is primarily the difference between snow accumulation and the melt and sublimation of snow and ice (ablation). Regional Climate Models (RCMs), which incorporate or are coupled to sophisticated representations of the mass and energy budgets associated with snow and ice surfaces, are now the primary source of ice-sheet SMB projections. The change in Greenland ice sheet SBM was obtained by fitting results from an RCM using input from several CMIP5 AOGCMs

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.climatechange2013.org/images/report/WG1AR5_Ch13SM_FINAL.pdf).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Available data include 10 geophysical sources that drive long-term changes in relative SSH:  
  
* 5 ice components (Greenland dynamic ice and surface mass balance, Antarctic dynamic ice and surface mass balance, and glaciers),  
  
* 3 ocean-related components, all of which are derived from CMIP5 models (dynamic SSH, global thermosteric SSH anomaly, and the inverse barometer effect from the atmosphere),  
  
* land water storage (also called terrestrial water), and  
  
* glacial isostatic adjustment (as a change in sea level relative to land). In addition to the relatively few fields actually used in the IPCC-AR5 figures, all individual components are available, both as maps of 20-year mean differences (always the 2081-2100 mean minus the 1986-2005 mean), and as time series with the 1986-2005 mean set as the common zero SSH anomaly value. Resource Watch displays the time series of total ensemble mean SSH for emissions scenario RCP 8.5; that same time series, along with those for lower, median, and upper projections, exist for RCP 2.6, 4.5, and 6.0 as well, along the projections from all 21 CMIP5 models. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

Universal Thermal Climate Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) provides a metric that identifies outdoor conditions that cause discomfort to people. It uses a combination of temperature, humidity, wind, and radiation to determine the stress (sweating, shivering, skin wetness, etc.) a person undergoes when exposed to outdoor conditions. UTCI comes from the ERA5-HEAT (Human thErmAl comforT) dataset from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). UTCI outputs are calculated globally (with the exception of Antarctica) and published on a monthly basis. UTCI is shown in degrees Celsius and presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25 degrees by 0.25 degrees, which is approximately 28 km x 28 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.

UTCI is a metric that provides critical information on how humans perceive the outdoor conditions they’re exposed to, and has implications for human health and well being. Extremes in temperatures, such as cold spells and heatwaves, cause an increase in morbidity and mortality and knowing where and when these occur is imperative. The UTCI enables people to better prepare and cope with temperature extremes.

ECMWF is an operational research institution that produces weather forecasts and data. They implement the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) which provides free and accessible climate information and data for a wide range of users.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The ERA5-HEAT (Human thErmAL comforT) dataset comes from the ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis data, which combines model data with observations from around the globe. The merging of modeled data with observations allows for a globally consistent and complete dataset, both geographically and through time. ERA5-HEAT calculates the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), which is computed from air temperature, humidity, wind speed, and radiation. Outputs of UTCI are provided in Kelvin on an hourly basis and at 0.25 degrees spatial resolution.

UTCI is a metric that relates human comfort/discomfort levels to outdoor conditions. It is a standard developed by the European Cooperation in Science and Technology (COST) Action 730 in 2009. It describes the air temperature of a reference outdoor environment that would evoke strain on the human body. It is calculated by an algorithm that takes into account a number of environmental variables, namely air temperature and relative humidity at 2 meters above ground, wind speed at 10 meters above ground, and the Mean Radiant Temperature (MRT). UTCI outputs are calculated globally (with the exception of Antarctica) for each hour and are provided in Kelvin. Outputs from ERA5 are available 2 to 3 months behind real time and the UTCI is calculated and published on a monthly basis.

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://rmets.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/gdj3.102).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for every year between 1979 and 2022 are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. We converted the original units from Kelvin to Celsius and averaged over time. See the documentation on how we processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_079_rw0_universal_thermal_climate_index).

title: Wood Fiber Concessions
description:
### Overview  
  
The Wood Fiber Concessions dataset shows public lands allocated by governments to private companies for the establishment of fast-growing tree plantations to produce timber for paper and paper products. The dataset is a compilation of concession data from the Republic of the Congo, Indonesia and Malaysia. Concession name, group and area in hectares (ha) are included in the Wood Fiber Concessions dataset. Wood Fiber Concessions data is typically from government agencies or nonprofits, although the data source and date vary by country. 

  
  
Wood fiber is a cellulose material extracted from trees and converted to wood pulp to make paper products. These products include paper, paperboard, cardboard and tissue. The year-round growing season and low cost of business has made tropical regions a popular wood fiber growing location. In these areas, it is common practice to clear land and plant fast-growing trees like the acacia. [Studies have shown](https://www.wri.org/blog/2017/07/drivers-deforestation-indonesia-inside-and-outside-concessions-areas) that these practices contribute to deforestation and [destruction of carbon-rich peat soils](https://www.wri.org/blog/2018/01/save-indonesias-carbon-rich-peatlands-start-mapping-them). Deforestation has many harmful impacts on the environment, including habitat destruction, erosion, air pollution and groundwater contamination. Understanding the locations and extent of wood fiber plantations provides information about potential environmental impacts. It can also be used to encourage farmers and businesses to use sustainable farming practices. 

  
  
The Wood Fiber Concessions dataset was generated by [Global Forest Watch (GFW)](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/about/), an organization established in 1997 by the [World Resources Institute (WRI)](https://www.wri.org/). WRI is an independent, non-governmental global research organization which seeks to create equity and prosperity through sustainable natural resource management. They provide data and research about climate, energy, food, forests, water, cities and oceans. GFW uses satellite data and cloud computing to monitor deforestation in near-real-time. Understanding when and where deforestation is occurring is critical for ending illegal deforestation, fires, and unsustainable practices. Farmers and landowners can use this data to protect their land and resources. Additionally, this data can be used by business owners and the public to monitor the environmental impacts of activities like logging, mining and farming.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The term “wood fiber concession” refers to an area allocated by a government to a company for industrial-scale fast-growing timber plantations. GFW generated the Wood Fiber Concessions dataset by compiling concession data from Republic of the Congo, Indonesia and Malaysia. Most locations in the dataset include the concession name, group and area (ha). 

  
  
Data for each country was collected from various sources, including from government agencies, environmental impact assessments and non-profits. The most common source was maps from forestry or agriculture-specific government agencies. This data was used to create polygons representing the locations and boundaries of concessions. Additional information, such as concession name and area, was added to the polygons as attributes. The Wood Fiber Concessions dataset was published in 2019, though the exact dates vary by country. Concession data for each country is available on the [GFW Open Data Portal](https://data.globalforestwatch.org/search?q=wood%20fiber). 

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Projected increases in minimum monthly winter air temperature -- U.S. (Sonoma County)
description: The California Basin Characterization Model (CA-BCM 2014) dataset provides historical and projected climate and hydrologic surfaces for the region that encompasses the state of California and all the streams that flow into it (California hydrologic region ). The CA-BCM 2014 applies a monthly regional water-balance model to simulate hydrologic responses to climate at the spatial resolution of a 270-m grid. The model has been calibrated using a total of 159 relatively unimpaired watersheds for the California region. The historical data is based on 800m PRISM data spatially downscaled to 270 m using the gradient-inverse distance squared approach (GIDS), and the projected climate surfaces include five CMIP-3 and nine CMIP-5 General Circulation Models under a range of emission scenarios or representative concentration pathways (RCPs) for a total of 18 futures that have been statistically downscaled using BCSD to 800 m and further downscaled using GIDS to 270 m for model application. The BCM approach uses a regional water balance model based on this high resolution precipitation and temperature as well as elevation, geology, and soils to produce surfaces for the following variables: precipitation, air temperature, April 1st snowpack, recharge, runoff, potential evapotranspiration (PET), actual evapotranspiration, and climatic water deficit, a parameter that is calculated as PET minus actual evapotranspiration. The revised modeling for the CA-BCM described in Flint et al. 2013, referenced below, includes the updated 800-m spatial resolution climate data from PRISM, the county level soils data (SSURGO) for the entire state, and more rigorous snow and PET calibrations for California. This dataset included updates to all the basin calibrations as well. The future climate projections included the original 4 projections that were revised with bias-corrections to the 800-m historical PRISM climate, plus an additional 3 projections from the CMIP3 dataset (IPCC 4th Assessment Report) and 11 projections from the CMIP5 datasets (IPCC 5th Assessment Report). These projections included a range of emissions scenarios and representative concentration pathways. All projections were processed by the BCM to provide hydrologic response to 18 future climates.

Projected Annual Average Temperature U.S. (RCP4.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps:

All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value.
All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value.
Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2.

The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

Female & Male Population Densities
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset provides estimates of population counts by age and sex for the year 2010. It uses national censuses and population registers for the year 2010. The global data is presented as gridded raster data with a 30 arc second resolution (about 1 km at the equator). This dataset was created by Columbia University’s Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN) and is the fourth version and 11th revision of the Gridded Population of the World (GPWv4) estimates.  
  
GPWv4 consists of estimates of age and sex disaggregated population as counts (number of persons per pixel) and densities (number of persons per km²).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Gridded Population of the World, Version 4 (GPWv4): Basic Demographic Characteristics, Revision 11 provides estimates of population counts by age and sex for the year 2010, consistent with national censuses and population registers. To estimate the male and female populations by age in 2010, the proportions of males and females in each five-year age group from ages 0-4 to ages 85+ for the given census year were calculated. These proportions were then applied to the 2010 estimates of the total population to obtain 2010 estimates of male and female populations by age.   
  
In some cases, the spatial resolution of the age and sex proportions was coarser than the resolution of the total population estimates to which they were applied. The population density rasters were created by dividing the population count rasters by the land area raster. The data files were produced as global rasters at 30 arc second (about 1 km at the equator) resolution. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data on male and female counts, and distribution of populations disaggregated by age, is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Air Quality: Methane (CH₄) Estimated Emissions
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) shows global anthropogenic methane (CH₄) emissions in 2018 from the following sectors: agriculture, animal agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions.  
  
Methane is a powerful, short-lived greenhouse gas, [emitted as a result of](https://scied.ucar.edu/methane) raising cattle and other ruminant animals, rice production, landfills, and energy generation. Methane is also an important precursor to ground-level ozone (O₃), an air pollutant and a major component of smog, which can worsen bronchitis and asthma and damage lung tissue.  
  
Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). Each compound shows the emissions by sector for up to 11 sectors, depending on the atmospheric compound. The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions dataset was developed by Emissions of Atmospheric Compounds and Compilation of Ancillary Data (ECCAD-AERIS). The data has global coverage at a 0.1 degree resolution, which is approximately 11 kilometers x 11 kilometers at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Emissions are provided as an annual sum for the years 2000 to 2019. This dataset shows annual emissions for the year 2018.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions are based on the data provided by the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research version 4.3.2 (EDGARv4.3.2) historical data. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. These trends were then disaggregated onto the same 0.1 degree grid as in EDGARv4.3.2. The sectors were then merged and aligned between the CEDS and EDGARv4.3.2 datasets. The 2011 to 2014 trends were applied to the EDGARv4.3.2 2010 emissions to estimate the emissions up to the year 2018. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/sites/default/files/2019-05/cams_emissions_general_document_apr2019_v6.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b).

title: Cumulative Climate Impacts on Marine Ecosystems
description:
This cumulative impact index ranging from ranging from 0 (no change) to 1 (maximum change) for the impact of climate change on oceans was calculated using sea surface temperature (SST), ocean productivity measured by chlorophyll (CHL), and ocean circulation by Ramirez et al. (2017). The data to calculate were from the longest time series of remote-sensing records (annual composites) on SST (1980-2014), CHL (1979-2014), and marine currents (1980-2014) available to provide finest-scale measurements of the impacts of climate change on the marine environment globally.   
  
Pixel basis, least-squares linear regression of annual information from SST, CHL, and the eastern and northern components of water speed were used for deriving the significance of temporal trends and its magnitudes (slopes; that is, annual changes in target features) over the past 3 decades. CHL data were sourced online as annual composites, whereas data on SST and marine currents were obtained on a monthly basis and averaged yearly to generate a linear relationship to extract slopes. This calculation was repeated for every pixel of the globe. These magnitudes were combined to obtain the spatially explicit Cumulative Impact Index.   
  
Different layers were first resampled following a bilinear interpolation procedure to match the spatial resolution of the coarsest SST product (that is, 1° grid). Absolute values for the slopes of obtained trends (a proxy to the magnitude of environmental changes) were then standardized to the maximum value to make all variables comparable. These relative values were subsequently added on a pixel basis and standardized again to the maximum value. In this way, researchers obtained a dimensionless index ranging from 0 (no change) to 1 (maximum change), thereby providing information about spatial heterogeneity in the magnitude of environmental changes and highlighting those marine areas that have undergone the largest changes in their environmental conditions. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Life Expectancy at Birth
description:
Life expectancy at birth is derived from male and female life expectancy at birth and compiled by the World Bank from sources such as (1) UN Population Division: World Population Prospects; (2) Census reports and other statistical publications from national statistical offices; (3) Eurostat: Demographic Statistics; (4) UN Statistical Division: Population and Vital Statistics Report (various years); (5) U.S. Census Bureau: International Database; and (6) Secretariat of the Pacific Community: Statistics and Demography. It is the average number of years a newborn is expected to live if mortality patterns at the time of its birth remain constant in the future. It reflects the overall mortality level of a population and summarizes the mortality pattern that prevails across all age groups in a given year. It is calculated in a period life table, which provides a snapshot of a population's mortality pattern at a given time. It therefore does not reflect the mortality pattern that a person actually experiences during his or her life, which can be calculated in a cohort life table. High mortality in young age groups significantly lowers the life expectancy at birth. But if a person survives his or her childhood of high mortality, he or she may live much longer. For example, in a population with a life expectancy at birth of 50, there may be few people dying at age 50. The life expectancy at birth may be low due to high childhood mortality, so that once a person survives his or her childhood, he or she may live much longer than 50 years. This data set of country-level figures is global in scope and spans 1960-present. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: [Archived] Water Stress Country Ranking
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](47053e23-7808-40d9-b4ae-1af73c5c8bab) as a replacement.**_
  
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the baseline water stress rating for countries and water basins at a national scale. Baseline water stress is a measure of the level of competition for available water and estimates the degree to which freshwater availability is an ongoing concern in a region. The dataset’s main focus is to include detailed and accurate information for the world’s 100 most populous river basins, as they are often areas where water stress is a large concern. Additionally, researchers grouped the final dataset into water usage by different sectors (agricultural, domestic, and industrial) to help understand where water stress in an area is coming from. The dataset was calculated by comparing weighted averages of water withdrawals in a region to the quantity of water available. The results were projected on a global map in five water stress risk categories: low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high.
  
  
Understanding water stress is integral for human wellbeing. Water is a limited resource and a necessity for life. Water stress can have serious environmental consequences, with damage occurring to natural ecosystems reliant on a steady water supply. Additionally, water stress can lead to human and business conflicts, particularly between industrial and agricultural users that rely on water supply for production.
  
  
This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) to assist companies, investors, and governments creating water use policies. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Researchers created this global dataset to include the 100 most populous river basins and all countries. Baseline water stress was calculated by dividing the weighted average water withdrawals in a region by the total blue freshwater available. To create the weighted average water withdrawals researchers used information on water withdrawals and divided each region into grid cells. Each grid cell was given a different weight based on the water withdrawals and water available within it. The grid cells were then combined to encompass different regions shown in the final dataset. Researchers further separated the dataset to view water usage in three different sectors (agricultural, domestic, and industrial).
  
  
Baseline water stress values were grouped into five categories when mapped: low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high. The water stress scores for each category are as follows: Low <1, low to medium 1-5, medium to high 5-10, high 10-20, and extremely high >20. Each category represents the risk of water stress in the area. Data for country boundaries was taken from the Natural Earth Data 10m Admin 0 – Countries dataset. Data on the extent of the 100 most populous river basins was taken from HydroSHEDS 30s Basin Outlines and Gridded Population of the World, v3, Future Estimates 2010 datasets. Gridded weights and source indicators (baseline water stress) were calculated using Aqueduct Global Maps 2.0.
  
  
The final dataset was created in tabular format and projected on a global map of the earth at a national scale. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [interannual variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat052-Aqueduct-Interannual-Variability) and [seasonal variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat053-Aqueduct-Seasonal-Variability) in water supply from the same dataset.

title: Population Below Income Poverty Line ($3.20)
description:
### Overview  
  
The Population Below Income Poverty Line ($3.20) dataset shows the percentage of the population living below a $3.20 a day poverty line in 2011 international prices. The $3.20 poverty line is derived from typical national poverty lines in countries classified as Lower Middle Income. The dataset is created by comparing the $3.20 poverty line to income and consumption data from each country. Income and consumption data allows researchers to determine the cost of living and the cost of goods and services in each country based on 2011 pricing. This is used to convert the $3.20 poverty line into local currencies and poverty rates. The dataset is published for low- and middle-income countries, countries eligible to receive World Bank loans, and recently graduated countries only. It is available for all years from 1967-present and has a national spatial resolution. 

  
  
The dataset was created by the World Bank as part of its internationally comparable poverty monitoring database. The database serves to monitor poverty rates for all countries and utilizes different poverty rates for different country income classifications. The World Bank Group is committed to reducing extreme poverty to 3 percent or less, globally, by 2030. Monitoring poverty is important on the global development agenda as well as on the national development agenda of many countries.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Population below Income Poverty Line ($3.20) dataset was created as part of the World Bank’s Poverty Measures of the Developing World database to calculate the poverty headcount ratio per country at a $3.20 a day poverty line. The poverty headcount ratio is the proportion of a population that lives below the poverty line. First, researchers determined the international poverty line to create a common standard of what “poverty” is. This was first done in the 1980’s by looking at academic papers on the economies of 22 developing countries and a poverty line of $1 a day was created. Since then new and updated international poverty lines have been created and as of 2015 the World Bank has used an international poverty line of $1.90 a day at 2011 purchasing power parity (PPP). This was created by averaging the national poverty lines of 15 of the poorest countries ranked by per capita consumption. The dataset shown here uses a more liberal poverty line of $3.20, which is based on low- and middle- income countries. It is based on 2011 PPP, which means the monetary value is representative of the cost of specific goods in each country as of 2011 and highlights the differences in absolute purchasing power between economies.
  
  
International poverty lines cannot be directly compared with poverty measured at national poverty lines in local currency, which reflect economy-specific decisions of poverty. To make them comparable and determine the rate of poverty in a country the international poverty line was applied to each country individually. To do this, income and consumption data from household surveys across 164 countries in six regions and 25 other high income countries were used to determine household living standards. The poverty line at 2011 PPP was converted into local currencies in 2011 prices and then converted to the prices of goods at the time of the relevant nationally representative household survey using the best available Consumer Price Index (CPI). CPI is a measure of the cost of consumer goods and services at a given time. Then the poverty rate was calculated by determining how much of the country's population fell below the $3.20 2011 PPP poverty line. The population living below the poverty line was then divided by the country’s total population and multiplied by 100 to create the final dataset. Nationally representative household surveys were conducted by national statistical offices or by private agencies under the supervision of government or international agencies and obtained from government statistical offices and World Bank Group operational departments. CPI data was primarily taken from the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF’s) International Financial Statistics.
  
  
To make national poverty rates comparable between countries they were calculated and shown for individual years, known as reference years. This required interpolating and extrapolating data for countries that lacked survey data for each year. This was done by adjusting the mean income or expenditure observed in a survey year by a country’s growth factor to estimate the unknown survey data in the reference year. 
  
  
For the full documentation, please see this [methodology document](http://iresearch.worldbank.org/PovcalNet/methodology.aspx) or click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information

title: Oil and Chemical Spill Incidents
description:
### Overview  
  
The Oil and Chemical Spill Incidents dataset shows the location of selected incidents that have occured from 1957 to present. The dataset shown on Resource Watch includes oil spills, chemical spills, and other incidents in which the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) Office of Response and Restoration (OR&R) has been active in assisting with the incident response. The dataset includes United States waters and some international locations show as point locations.

  
  
OR&R is the federal U.S. government organization with expertise in preparing for, evaluating, and responding to threats to coastal environments, including oil and chemical spills, releases from hazardous waste sites, and marine debris. They are responsible for responding to and providing scientific support to federal on-scene coordinators for these incidents. The dataset is intended to provide public access to the history of incidents that have occured. It can be used to show trends and the long term effects of spills.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Oil and Chemical Spill Incidents dataset was created by using data from reports created by NOAA's Office of Response and Restoration (OR&R). These reports are present for all oil, chemical, and other incidents that OR&R provided scientific support for. From each report the name, date, location (longitude/latitude), type of threat, and a brief description were cataloged in the Raw Incident dataset.

title: Ocean Dissolved Oxygen Concentration
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows global daily and monthly mean dissolved oxygen (O₂) concentrations in seawater from the surface to 5.1 meters in depth. The data are a product of the Global Ocean and Biogeochemistry Analysis system, a global biogeochemical simulation using the [PISCES model](https://www.nemo-ocean.eu/framework/components/engines) and are displayed at a 0.25° by 0.25° resolution. 

  
  
Oxygen is critical to the health of the ocean. It structures aquatic ecosystems, impacts the biogeochemical cycling of carbon, nitrogen and other key elements, and is a fundamental requirement for marine life. However, climate change and human activity are affecting the ocean oxygen cycle. Through ocean circulation, specific parts of the ocean are delivered high concentrations of nutrients, upwelling from nutrient rich polar deep water. The nutrients fuel a naturally, highly productive state, driving phytoplankton blooms that oxygenate the surface ocean, and supporting large fish aggregations. This high level of productivity can lead to deoxygenation of the internal ocean through respiration as fish consume the plant matter and produce CO₂. A similar situation, known as coastal eutrophication, can occur in bays, semi enclosed seas, and coastal areas due to the anthropogenic addition of nutrients, including nitrates and phosphates. Coastal eutrophication oxygenates the surface ocean, and can drive the deoxygenation of the seafloor of the coastal area as the plant matter is consumed. 

  
  
 Since the 1960s, the area of low oxygen zones in the open ocean has [increased by 4.5 million km²](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/359/6371/eaam7240). As the surface ocean continues to warm due to climate change, the oxygen minimum zones in the internal ocean will continue to grow, significantly impacting a range of habitats and globally important fish stocks. More accurate predictions of ocean deoxygenation, as well as accurate oxygen measurements with appropriate temporal resolution and adequate spatial coverage in the marine environment are needed to document the current status of our ocean, to track changing conditions, to build and validate models that can project future oxygen levels, and to develop strategies to slow and reverse deoxygenation.

   
  
The [Copernicus Marine Service](https://marine.copernicus.eu/) is the marine component of the Copernicus Programme of the European Union. It provides free, regular and systematic authoritative information on the state of the ocean, on a global and regional scale. It is funded by the European Commission (EC) and implemented by [Mercator-Ocean International](https://www.mercator-ocean.fr/). It is designed to serve policy and commitments related to Ocean Governance, to cater for the needs of society at large for global ocean knowledge and to boost the Blue Economy across all maritime sectors by providing free-of-charge state-of-the-art ocean data and information.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The data shown are based on the PISCES biogeochemical model available on the [Nucleus for European Modelling of the Ocean (NEMO)](https://www.nemo-ocean.eu/) modelling platform. The model includes 24 predictor variables and simulates biogeochemical cycles of oxygen, carbon, and the main nutrients controlling phytoplankton growth (nitrate, ammonium, phosphate, silicic acid, and iron). Mean nutrient concentrations are interpolated on a standard regular grid in NetCDF format. The output product is validated by comparing systematically the biogeochemical modeled fields with available observations datasets. The data isdisplayed with a 1/4 degree horizontal resolution with regular longitude/latitude equirectangular projection. 

  
  
For the full documentation and additional information about the PISCES model, please see the source [methodology](http://marine.copernicus.eu/documents/QUID/CMEMS-GLO-QUID-001-028.pdf).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows daily and monthly dissolved oxygen concentration averaged from a depth of 0 to 5.1 meters. CMEMS provides 50 vertical levels covering a depth profile of 0 to 5500 meters from the surface. Resource Watch also shows CMEMS averages for [nitrates](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92327c78-a473-402b-8edf-409869823216) and [phosphates](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/f1aa9ec7-c3b6-441c-b395-96fc796b7612). Additional biogeochemical fields for chlorophyll concentration, silicate, dissolved iron, primary production, phytoplankton, pH, and surface partial pressure of carbon dioxide are also included in the Global Ocean and Biogeochemistry Analysis and Forecast system.   
  

For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/ocn_020_nrt_rw0_nutrient_mole_concentration).

title: Human Settlement Grid
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the global spatial distribution of settlement classifications related to the land area’s degree of urbanization. It is created with a combination of data on population and built-up density. The data covers 1975, 1990, 2000, and 2015 with a 1 kilometer (km) resolution, and was created by the European Commission Joint Research Centre (EC JRC).

  
  
This dataset classifies land into seven classifications that range from urban city to low-density rural areas. Cells that contain over 50% water or are completely unpopulated are excluded. The classifications are presented in grid-level terms with the associated municipal level terms. For example, grid-level term *urban center* corresponds with municipal level term *city*. 

  
  
This dataset is part of a larger project called the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHS), which produces global spatial information and analytics to describe human presence on earth. GHS is used as a base measurement to support multiple projects, like the Geo Human Planet Initiative (HPI) and the European Union’s 2030 Development Agenda.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The final dataset was created using the information on population density, the share of built-up area, and the number of contiguous grid cells sharing similar settlement classifications. This dataset is derived from a combination of two input datasets: Landsat image data processing (GHS-BUILT) and GHS population density dataset (GHS-POP). GHS-BUILT shows built-up density and is based on remote sensing image data from the Global Land Survey’s (GLS) Landsat image database. GHS-POP depicts the residential density and distribution of population based on the Center for International Earth Science Information Network’s (CIESIN) Gridded Population of the World, version 4.10 (GPWv4.10). Land data was extracted from the [Global ADMinstrative Map 2.8](https://gadm.org/data.html) and the [Global Surface Water Occurrence](https://global-surface-water.appspot.com/download). Name data was collected OpenStreetMaps and filtered by EUROSTAT.

  
  
GHS-POP and GHS-BUILT were combined to create the final product on settlement classifications presented at a spatial resolution of 1 km. The final dataset has grid cells classified into seven settlement classifications ranging from city (urban centers)  to very low-density areas (rural land). 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://ghsl.jrc.ec.europa.eu/documents/GHSL_Data_Package_2019.pdf).

Maize, Rice, Soybean, and Wheat Yield Trends
description:
### Overview  
  
The Maize, Rice, Soybean, and Wheat Yield Trends dataset shows the average annual change in crop yield from 1989-2008. Agricultural crop yield is the amount of crop harvested per area of land. It is used to measure a crop’s performance. This study used approximately 1.8 million agricultural census reports from 13,500 political units around the world to determine how crop yield changed over time. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes, which is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.”
  
  
Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels and increased biofuel demand. In order to meet projected demand, [crop production needs to double by 2050](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms2296#MOESM1532). Improving crop yield, instead of clearing new land for agriculture, is one of the preferred solutions. In many areas, yield is stagnant or has collapsed entirely. Understanding where improvement is most needed can guide new agricultural investments. It is also important to identify and continue improving yield of high-performing crops and regions.  

  
  
This dataset was produced by EarthStat, a collaboration between the Global Landscapes Initiative (GLI) at the University of Minnesota’s Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE) and the Land Use and Global Environment (LUGE) lab at the University of British Columbia (UBC). EarthStat’s mission is to provide data on the global food system to help others make science-based decisions. The GLI is a scientific initiative that develops and applies tools to characterize global land use and evaluate global agricultural supply and demand trends. The LUGE lab is a research group that studies links between land use, global environmental change, and food security.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Approximately 1.8 million census reports were used to determine yield of the four crops for the years between 1989 and 2008. Crop yield is the ratio of production (kilograms) and harvested area (hectares). According to the UN’s [Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)](http://www.fao.org/waicent/faostat/agricult/pr_ele-e.htm), production is the amount of crop harvested. The harvested area is the area from which the crop is gathered. National-level data used in this study was provided by the [FAO](http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#home), who collects data from the member countries’ statistical offices. At the time of the study, the FAO had crop data for 226 nations. In addition to national-level data, the study also used subnational data for the 51 countries that account for more than 70% of global production/harvested area for each of the four crops. Data was available at the state/province level for all 51 countries and county/district/município/department level for an additional 17 countries. This data was collected from these countries’ agricultural and statistical bureaus. 

  
  
According to the data provider, studies have used linear regression to project future crop yields. As such, the annual crop yields in this study (one data point per year) were linearly regressed to calculate the average change in yield from 1989-2008. A linear regression is a line modeled to fit the shape of a group of data points. The slope of the line gives the rate of change–in this case, the average yield change over the observed period. This calculation was performed for each crop at each political unit. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0066428#pone.0066428.s017).

description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](fe9b286f-4b28-409a-85f5-2e81b2bd5056) as a replacement.**_
  
The social and economic vulnerability data set was produced for the Reefs at Risk project by World Resources Institute (WRI) and classifies the Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) for 108 coral reef countries and territories according to an index of their reef dependence, adaptive capacity, and social vulnerability. Results are presented as quartiles, with 27 countries/territories classified in each of 4 categories (low, medium, high, and very high for reef dependence and social vulnerability; very low, low, medium, and high for adaptive capacity). The Reef Dependence index is based on the following inputs: reef-associated population, reef fisheries employment, reef-associated exports, nutritional dependence on fish and seafood, reef-associated tourism, and shoreline protection. The Adaptive Capacity index is based on the following inputs: economic resources, education, health (expressed as life expectancy), governance, access to markets, and agricultural resources. The Social Vulnerability index is the result of the combination of the Reef Dependence index, Adaptive Capacity index, and Exposure to Reef Threats (i.e., the Reefs at Risk integrated local threat index). The Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) for uninhabited and sparsely inhabited territories with coral reefs are also included in this shapefile, but are not included in the indices. The purpose of this data set is to provide a comparative analysis of coral reef countries and territories according to their reef dependence, adaptive capacity, and social and economic vulnerability to reef loss. Results were compiled at the national level, or in some cases the subnational level where data were available. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Projected Heating Degree Day U.S. (RCP4.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual heating degree days (HDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. HDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is below 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual HDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. HDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, HDD are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for heating buildings.

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual HDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily HDDs were calculated by subtracting daily average temperature values from the baseline temperature of 65°F. If the daily average temperature was above 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual HDD was calculated by summing all daily HDD values over a given year. Annual HDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in heating degree days.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

Projected Extreme Heat Days (RCP4.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset shows the change in the average number of days of extreme heat at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme heat day is a day where the maximum temperature is greater than the 99th percentile maximum temperature during the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. Temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, an increased quantity of extreme heat days can lead to human and ecosystem threats caused by more frequent, more intense, and longer heat waves.

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The average number of extreme heat days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily maximum temperature values for a given year and summing the number of days where the maximum temperature was greater than the 99th percentile temperature during the baseline period. The number of extreme heat days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in extreme heat days. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Gross Domestic Product Per Capita
description:
### Overview  
  
Gross domestic product (GDP) per capita is a key economic indicator that measures the monetary value of goods and services provided per person. The gridded GDP per capita dataset used national GDP, gridded population data, and other factors to estimate GDP per capita at a 5 arc-minute resolution for each year from 1990 to 2015. This gridded GDP per capita dataset is important because it can be used for research at the sub-national level.   
  
GDP per capita measurements are in purchasing power parity (PPP) in 2011 U.S. dollars. The data was created at Aalto University. The authors also created the [gridded GDP](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc073-Gridded-GDP) data set.  
  
### Methodology  
  
To create a high resolution, complete picture of GDP per capita, the author calculated it using the World Bank Development Indicators database. For missing countries, they used data from the Central Intelligence Agency World Factbook. The temporal coverage of both the national and sub-national data varied considerably. To fill in the missing values, temporal interpolation and extrapolation approaches were used.  
  
To be consistent between the sub-national and national datasets, and to ensure the data set would represent official national statistics, the authors did not use the sub-national GDP per capita directly, but instead used the sub-national data to scale national GDP per capita. This was done for each year by first calculating population-weighted national GDP per capita from sub-national GDP per capita data and the HYDE 3.2 population data set. This output was then used in each sub-national unit to calculate the ratio between population-weighted national GDP and reported sub-national GDP. The final sub-national GDP per capita (in PPP) was calculated by multiplying the ratio with the reported national GDP per capita. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: U.S. Land Cover
description:
The National Land Cover Database products are created through a cooperative project conducted by the Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics (MRLC) Consortium. The MRLC Consortium is a partnership of Federal agencies (www.mrlc.gov), consisting of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the U.S. Department of Agriculture - Forest Service (USDA-FS), the National Park Service (NPS), the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS). 

National Land Cover Database 2011 (NLCD 2011) is the most recent national land cover product created by the MRLC Consortium. NLCD 2011 provides - for the first time - the capability to assess wall-to-wall, spatially explicit, national land cover changes and trends across the United States from 2001 to 2011. As with two previous NLCD land cover products NLCD 2011 keeps the same 16-class land cover classification scheme that has been applied consistently across the United States at a spatial resolution of 30 meters. NLCD 2011 is based primarily on a decision-tree classification of circa 2011 Landsat satellite data. 

National Land Cover Database 2006 (NLCD 2006) is a 16-class land cover classification scheme that has been applied consistently across the conterminous United States at a spatial resolution of 30 meters. NLCD 2006 is based primarily on a decision-tree classification of circa 2006 Landsat satellite data. NLCD 2006 also quantifies land cover change between the years 2001 to 2006. The NLCD2006 land cover change product was generated by comparing spectral characteristics of Landsat imagery between 2001 and 2006, on an individual path/row basis, using protocols to identify and label change based on the trajectory from NLCD 2001 products. 

National Land Cover Database 2001 (NLCD 2001) is a 16-class (additional four classes in Alaska only) land cover classification scheme that has been applied consistently across all 50 United States and Puerto Rico at a spatial resolution of 30 meters. NLCD 2001 is based primarily on a decision-tree classification of circa 2001 Landsat satellite data. NLCD 2001 improves on NLCD92 in that it is comprised of three different elements: land cover, percent developed impervious surface and percent tree canopy density.

title: Child Malnutrition
description:
### Overview  
  
The child malnutrition datasat shows child malnutrition estimates for 152 countries in 2018. This dataset demonstrates child malnutrition using five indicators: stunting, wasting, severe wasting, underweight, and overweight among children under 5 years old. The indicators are based on height, weight, and age ratios of children compared to World Health Organization (WHO) Growth Standards. The dataset utilizes the information collected from 854 household nutritional surveys and is presented in tabular format on a global scale.

  
  
The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), UN World Health Organization (WHO), and World Bank interagency team regularly update this dataset. Malnutrition robs children’s futures and hinders their growth, chance of survival, and development. Ultimately, this severely reduces their ability to contribute to their local communities and the world as a whole. According to UNICEF, nearly half of all deaths in children under five are attributable to undernutrition. Analysis from this dataset reveals that malnutrition rates remain alarmingly high. To improve children’s nutrition requires multi-sectoral programming with long term planning strategies. Regular data collection is essential to monitor trends and progress, and to raise awareness of nutritional problems. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was created using estimates from 854 nationally representative household nutritional surveys that were reviewed against a set of quality control criteria. These surveys are typically carried out every three to five years, so yearly estimates were created using data trends. Survey data was checked for validity and consistency. Additionally, to ensure that survey estimates were comparable over time, survey data was compared to an international standard reference population, the WHO Child Growth Standards. 

  
  
The WHO Child Growth Standards were used to compare five malnutrition indicators to those collected in surveys. Survey data for each indicator was presented using z-scores (how many standard deviations away from the mean) based on the WHO Child Growth Standards. For example, stunting is calculated as the proportion of children with height-for-age below two standard deviation of the reference population based on WHO Child Growth Standards. 

  
  


For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://data.unicef.org/resources/dataset/malnutrition-data/).   
  
### Additional Information

Additional data for global and regional level malnutrition, as well as indicator-specific national and disaggregated data are also available from the data provider. title: U.S. Flood Hazards
description:
The National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) is a digital database that contains flood hazard mapping data from FEMA’s National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). This map data is derived from Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) databases and Letters of Map Revision (LOMRs).The NFHL is for community officials and members looking to view effective regulatory flood hazard information in a Geographic Information Systems (GIS) application.

The NFHL provides users with the ability to determine the flood zone, base flood elevation and floodway status for a particular geographic location. It also has National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) community information, map panel information, cross section and hydraulic structure information, Coastal Barrier Resource System information (if applicable) and base map information, such as road, stream and public land survey data.  A full list of the layers available in the NFHL may be found in the NFHL GIS Services User Guide.

The NFHL data set represents the current effective flood risk data for those parts of the country where maps have been modernized. It is a compilation of effective Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) databases and Letters of Map Revision (LOMR). The NFHL is updated as new data reaches its designated effective date and becomes valid for regulatory use under the NFIP.

Political Rights and Civil Liberties Index
description:
Freedom in the World is Freedom House’s flagship annual report, assessing the condition of political rights and civil liberties around the world. It is composed of numerical ratings and supporting descriptive texts for 195 countries and 14 territories. Freedom in the World has been published since 1973, allowing Freedom House to track global trends in freedom over more than 40 years. External analysts assess the 209 countries and territories using a combination of on-the-ground research, consultations with local contacts, and information from news articles, nongovernmental organizations, governments, and a variety of other sources. Expert advisers and regional specialists then vet the analysts’ conclusions. The final product represents the consensus of the analysts, advisers, and Freedom House staff. For each country and territory, Freedom in the World analyzes the electoral process, political pluralism and participation, the functioning of the government, freedom of expression and of belief, associational and organizational rights, the rule of law, and personal autonomy and individual rights. A country or territory is assigned 2 ratings (7 to 1)—one for political rights and one for civil liberties—based on its total scores for the political rights and civil liberties questions. Each rating of 1 through 7, with 1 representing the greatest degree of freedom and 7 the smallest degree of freedom, corresponds to a specific range of total scores. The average of a country’s or territory’s political rights and civil liberties ratings is called the Freedom Rating, and it is this figure that determines the status of free (1.0 to 2.5), partly free (3.0 to 5.0), or not free (5.5 to 7.0).
