title: Relative Change in Crop Yield
description:
### Overview  
  
Relative change in crop yield shows climate projections for crop yield at the national and sub-national levels under different concentration pathways (RCP 4.5 and 8.5). Data is aggregated annually for either national or sub-national boundaries and depict changes in crop yield over time from 2015 through 2050. Changes in yield are compared to the reference period of 1986-2006 and are shown in percentages.

Understanding how climate change will affect crop yields is important for agricultural planning, food security, and global commodity flows. This dataset provides needed information on how climate change will impact yield under several emissions scenarios at the country and provincial levels and for near- and longer-term timeframes. The global economy is intimately tied to agricultural production, and this provides insight into future changes that will have impact on global systems.

Climate Analytics is dedicated to advancing scientific literacy of climate change and providing support and capacity building to stakeholders. They support science-based policy to enable sustainable development and provide solutions to climate change policy challenges.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Input data for crop yield change uses greenhouse gas concentration scenarios derived from the Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) framework, which was developed within the Coupled Intercomparison Modeling Project 5 (CMIP5) and is widely used in the climate modeling community. RCP 4.5 depicts an intermediate scenario whereas 8.5 represents a high emissions pathway. Other data is derived from the Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project (ISIMIP), which provides changes in biophysical systems and extreme events.
 
Climate projections for crop yield were modeled for different emissions scenarios from 2015 to 2100 and are compared against the baseline period of 1986-2006. Results show the annual average changes in crop yield over the area of interest (national/sub-national levels). Projections of future impacts to changes in crop yield are calculated assuming that socio-economic (population, land-use, etc.) factors remain constant at 2005 levels.
 
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://climate-impact-explorer.climateanalytics.org/methodology/).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Our data catalog also shows Relative Humidity data from Climate Analytics. Additional projections for other crops, impacts, emissions scenarios, and timeframes are also produced by Climate Analytics. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/foo_069_rw0_relative_change_crop_yield). This data has been mapped on our data catalog by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

title: Recent Internal Displacement from Conflict, Natural Disasters, and Development
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset tracks the number of people who have been internally displaced recently due to conflict, natural disasters, or development projects worldwide, and is updated daily. ”Internal displacement” refers to the forced movement of people within the country that they live in. Millions of people are forced to flee their homes each year due to conflict, violence, development projects, disasters, and climate change, and remain displaced within their countries of residence.
  
  

Internally displaced persons (IDPs) can include both citizens and other habitual residents of the country, such as stateless persons. IDPs can include, but are not limited to
  
  
- families caught between warring parties who had to flee their homes due to continuous attacks or threats;
  
  
- residents of neighborhoods that have become unsafe or uninhabitable due to the impacts of weather-related, geophysical, or technological hazards;
  
  
- indigenous communities forced from their ancestral lands to make way for the construction of dams and other infrastructure projects;
  
  
- families pushed to leave their homes by constant harassment by local criminal gangs;
  
  
- communities whose livelihoods have been severely impacted by drought and are unable to feed their families; and
  
  
- communities from coastal, mountainous, or arid regions whose land and livelihoods were lost because of gradual environmental degradation linked to the impacts of climate change.
  
  

Some of the typical needs and protection risks that arise in internal displacement include family separation, loss of documentation, loss of property, and further exposure to the risk of continued displacement.
  
  

This dataset is produced by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) with the aim of informing policy and operational decisions in order to reduce the risk of future displacement and improve the lives of IDPs worldwide. Resource Watch also shows IDMC estimates of the number of people displaced annually, aggregated to the national level. This data is available for displacements due to [natural disasters](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522ef9945f7-d934-4a88-a02a-570f14fffefc%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25223bda62f1-7146-4dd5-bf3f-d3bfae26d0d7%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062a) and due to [conflict](https://preproduction.resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%25226974833b-004e-4b24-bdbc-ffbb779c1496%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%2522cb5daeb3-80ef-4e6e-8ca8-5ed0d6170b3b%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062b).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Country analysts monitor displacements in near real-time on an event-by-event basis after IDMC learns of their occurrence. For each event, information from a wide variety of different sources is compiled, generating the most comprehensive and reliable displacement estimate. These sources include national and subnational government authorities, UN agencies and other international organizations, related global databases, civil society organizations, news media outlets, and other entities. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.internal-displacement.org/database/methodology).

This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis and Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, the U.S. Geological Survey, and  the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, measures areas of tree cover gain across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at 30 × 30 m resolution, displayed as a 12-year cumulative layer. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+) sensor. Over 600,000 Landsat 7 images were compiled and analyzed using Google Earth Engine, a cloud platform for Earth observation and data analysis. The clear land surface observations (30 × 30 m pixels) in the satellite images were assembled, and a supervised learning algorithm was then applied to identify per pixel tree cover gain. Tree cover gain was defined as the establishment of tree canopy at the Landsat pixel scale in an area that previously had no tree cover. Tree cover gain may indicate a number of potential activities, including natural forest growth or the crop rotation cycle of tree plantations. The tree cover canopy density of the displayed data is >50%. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Multidimensional Poverty Index
description:
The UN Development Programme (UNDP) compiles the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) as part of its Human Development Report initiative. First published in 2010, the MPI identifies multiple deprivations at the household level in health, education, and standard of living. It uses microdata from household surveys, and—unlike the Inequality-Adjusted Human Development Index—all the indicators needed to construct the measure must come from the same survey. Each person in a given household is classified as poor or nonpoor depending on the weighted number of deprivations his or her household experiences. These data are then aggregated into the national measure of poverty. The MPI reflects both the prevalence of multidimensional deprivation and its intensity—the percentage of simultaneous deprivations poor people experience. It can be used to create a comprehensive picture of people living in poverty and permits comparisons both across countries, regions, and the world and within countries by ethnic group, urban, or rural location, as well as other key household and community characteristics. The MPI offers a valuable complement to income-based poverty measures. Indicators shown in the MPI include the following: (1) health: nutrition and child mortality; (2) education: years of schooling and children enrolled; and (3) standard of living: cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, and assets. The MPI is calculated by multiplying the incidence of poverty by the intensity of poverty. The incidence of poverty is the proportion of people considered to experience multidimensional poverty, in other words, that are considered deprived in at least one-third of the MPI's weighted indicators. The intensity of multidimensional poverty is the weighted average number of deprivations poor people experience at the same time. The main data sources of the MPI are the Macro Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) of the Inner City Fund (ICF) and the Multiple Indicators Cluster Survey (MICS) of the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). The 2020 Human Development Report (HDR) presents estimates for 107 countries—28
low income, 76 middle income, and 3 high income—and 5.9 billion people in developing regions. About 1.3 billion people in the 107 developing countries covered—22% of their entire population—lived in multidimensional poverty. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Urban Population
description:
### Overview  
  
The Urban Population dataset shows the number of people living in urban areas, expressed as a percentage of the total national population. Urban areas were determined by national statistics offices in each country and no universal definition is used to describe what constitutes an urban area. The dataset is presented at a national resolution for each year between 1960 and present.

  
  
Urban growth is closely related to the three dimensions of sustainable development: social, economic, and environmental. Well-managed urbanization, informed by an understanding of population trends over the long run, can help to maximize the benefits of high levels of density while minimizing environmental degradation and other potential adverse impacts of a growing number of city dwellers. In principle, cities offer a more favorable setting for the resolution of social and environmental problems than rural areas. Cities generate jobs and income, and deliver education, health care and other services. Cities also present opportunities for social mobilization and women's empowerment. This dataset provides the basis for understanding these trends in urbanization and gives background for governments to implement policies related to these changes.

  
  
This dataset was released by the United Nations Population Division (UNPD) and distributed by the World Bank Group. The Urban Population dataset is a part of World Development Indicators (WDI), the Work Bank’s primary collection of development indicators, compiled from officially recognized international sources. It presents the most current and accurate global development data available, and includes national, regional and global estimates.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Urban population was determined by using World Bank Group population estimates and urban ratios from the UN World Urbanization Prospects. Urban ratios were created with data largely from national censuses and population registers, which typically supplied complete counts of both the total population in a country and the total population living in urban areas. The urban ratio is defined by the ratio of the total population that lives in urban areas compared to rural areas. This was combined with national population estimates to determine the percentage of the total population living in urban areas.

  
  
In some cases, census data was not available for every year. In order to create yearly estimates, interpolation or extrapolation based on the data available was used. The urban population estimates used to create the urban ratio were based on the definitions used for statistical purposes by the countries and areas themselves. No universal definition for urban was used. Depending on the country, any combination of the following characteristics may have been used to distinguish urban and rural areas: information about administrative designations, population size or density, demographics, economic characteristics, and functional characteristics (existence of paved streets, water supply systems, etc.). No independent adjustment of national statistics were undertaken unless it was clear that the definitions used by a given country had changed over time in ways that would have led to inconsistencies. 

  
  
Despite efforts to avoid inconsistencies within countries, it was not always possible to adjust the available data in ways that ensured consistency. In some cases, inconsistencies remained because the data needed to make the necessary adjustments were lacking. In cases where adjustment was possible, every effort was made to adjust earlier data so that they conformed to the most recent definition.  

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://population.un.org/wup/Publications/Files/WUP2018-Methodology.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the same time period is available for rural population rates. The results can be viewed by country development groups, geographic regions (i.e., Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean, Northern America and Oceania), income groups, and 21 geographic subregions. Additionally, estimates and projections are  available on the population of urban agglomerations with 300,000 inhabitants or more in 2018 for the period between 1950 and 2035.  For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Aqueduct Coastal Flood Risk
description:
### Overview  
  
Coastal flood risk measures the percentage of the population expected to be affected by coastal flooding in an average year, accounting for existing flood-protection standards. Higher values indicate that a greater proportion of the population is expected to be impacted by coastal floods on average. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<0.0009‬%) to extremely high (>0.2%).

  
  
Flood risk was assessed using hazard (inundation caused by storm surge), exposure (population in flood zone), and vulnerability. The existing level of flood protection was also incorporated into the risk calculation. It is important to note that this indicator represents flood risk not in terms of maximum possible impact but rather as average annual impact. The impacts from infrequent, extreme flood years were averaged with more common, less newsworthy flood years to produce the “expected annual affected population.”  Values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6).
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data on the population impacted by coastal floods were provided by Aqueduct Floods  (Ward et al. forthcoming). Flood risk was simulated using a cascade of models within the Global Flood Risk with IMAGE Scenarios (GLOFRIS) modeling framework [(Winsemius et al. 2013)](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-17-1871-2013). Coastal hazard maps were derived using Global Tide and Surge Reanalysis (GTSR) [(Muis et al., 2016)](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms11969) datasets from 1974-2014.The coastal flood hazard is represented by inundation maps showing the flood extent and depth for floods of several return periods (2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, and 1000 years) at a horizontal resolution of 5’x5’ (regridded to 30”x30”). Exposure is represented by gridded maps of 2010 population count per cell at a horizontal resolution of 30” x 30”. Vulnerability is represented as a binary condition: people are either affected or they are not. Estimates of flood protection standards come from the FLOPROS model.

  
  
The expected annual affected population was calculated using a risk curve [(Meyer et al. 2009)](https://doi.org/10.1897/IEAM_2008-031.1). To create the curve, the return periods were first converted into probabilities (i.e., 1/return period) and then plotted on the x-axis against the impacted population. Next, flood protection (return year converted to probability) was added to the graph as a vertical line. All impacts that fell to the right of the flood protection line (i.e., impacted by smaller floods) were assumed to be protected against floods and were removed from the calculation. The expected annual affected population was calculated by integrating the area under the curve to the left of the flood protection line.

  
  
The expected annual affected population was divided by total population to calculate the percent of the population expected to be affected annually by riverine floods.

  
  
Finally, raw coastal flood risk values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw coastal flood risk values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.

- Low (0-1): < 0 to 9 in 1,000,000 people
- Low to medium (1-2): 9 in 1,000,000 to 7 in 100,000 people
- Medium to high (2-3): 7 in 100,000 to 3 in 10,000 people
- High (3-4): 3 in 10,000 people to 2 in 1,000 people
- Extremely high (4-5): > 2 in 1,000 people

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: Projected Change in Frost Free Season
description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af).

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Nighttime Lights 2012 and 2016
description:
The "Earth at Night" map images were generated by National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) using the Suomi National Polar-Orbiting Partnership (Suomi NPP) satellite, managed by NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Suomi NPP observes nearly every location on Earth at roughly 1:30 p.m. and 1:30 a.m. (local time) each day, as it images the planet in vertical 3,000 km (2,000-mile) strips from pole to pole. The satellite’s workhorse instrument is the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), which detects photons of light reflected from the Earth’s surface and atmosphere in 22 different wavelengths. The final Earth at Night products show the areas of man-made visible and infrared light in the world at night, excluding moonlight, fires, and other natural sources of light. Areas with the brightest light points tend to be population centers and are often located in coastal areas. Earth at Night maps are available for the years 2012 and 2016, in both color and grayscale, in both JPEG and GeoTIFF formats and with resolution from 500 m to 3 km. The 2016 images were processed using a compositing technique that selected the best cloud-free nights in each month over each land mass. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Plastic density in the oceans
description:
### Overview  
  
The dataset represents the count (pieces per square kilometer) and weight (grams per square kilometer) densities of plastic particles floating in the ocean. The data was created from an oceanographic model of floating debris dispersal and calibrated using data from surveys done during 24 expeditions conducted from 2007-2013. The results have been adjusted for a variety of factors like particle fragmentation and wind driven mixing of water. The data is presented in four particle size categories ranging from 0.33 millimeters to >200 millimeters. The final results are shown in raster format at a spatial resolution of 20 kilometers. 
  
  

Plastic pollution is globally distributed across all oceans and is regarded as a major health issue for marine and human life. As plastic degrades it forms microplastics that are often consumed by marine fauna, slowly working up the food chain. In addition, floating plastics can move across oceans and transport species to non-native regions. 
  
  

This study was conducted to help countries understand their impacts on the ocean and to be used in implementing plastic waste reduction policies. It was authored by researchers from a variety of organizations and funded by an array of environmental and educational groups. The data has global coverage and is available at a spatial resolution of 0.2° or about 20 kilometers.  
  
### Methodology  
  
To gather the mass and count of the ocean’s plastics, the researchers conducted 24 expeditions (2007–2013) across all five subtropical gyres, coastal Australia, Bay of Bengal, and the Mediterranean Sea. During these expeditions 680 surface net tows and 891 visual survey transects of large plastic debris were conducted. Surface net tows were done using a mesh size of 0.33 millimeters towed at 0.5 to 2 meters below the ocean surface for 15 to 60 minutes. Visual surveys were carried out using dedicated observers viewing 20 meter sections next to the boat noting large floating debris. Debris observations were broken into nine categories, four categories for fishing-related debris: buoy, line, net, and other fishing gear, and five categories for other plastics: bucket, bottle, foamed polystyrene, bag/film, or miscellaneous plastics. All 1,571 mesh and visual surveys included data on plastic counts and 1,333 of them also included data on debris weight.
  
  

The data was used to create debris estimates and calibrate an oceanographic model based on water movement to show the dispersal of floating debris. The model used to describe oceanic currents was the US Navy’s Hybrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM). This was combined with a Lagrangian particle-tracking model Pol3DD to mimic how plastic particles move through the ocean. The model assumes that amounts of plastic entering the ocean depends on three principal variables: watershed outfalls, population density, and maritime activity. The results were adjusted to compensate for wind driven mixing of the surface layer that forces plastic particles below the surface. Additionally, conservative estimates for particle fragmentation rates were used when determining particle count. Through this methodology, estimated values were generated for the count and weight of ocean plastic in four size classes: 0.33-1.0 millimeters, 1.01-4.75 millimeters, 4.76-200 millimeters, and >200 millimeters.
  
  

For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0111913).

description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c29aee50-a46f-4c10-a8b1-152e4821be81) as a replacement.**_
  
The access-to-electricity data are released through the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) database and collected among different sources: demographic and health surveys (DHSs) and living standards measurement surveys (LSMSs), multi-indicator cluster surveys (MICSs), the World Health Survey (WHS), other nationally developed and implemented surveys, and various government agencies (e.g., ministries of energy and utilities). Given the low frequency and the regional distribution of some surveys, a number of countries have gaps in available data. To develop the historical evolution and starting point of electrification rates, a simple modeling approach was adopted to fill in the missing data points: around 1990, around 2000, and around 2010. Therefore, a country can have a continuum of 0 to 3 data points. There are 42 countries with 0 data points, and the weighted regional average was used as an estimate for electrification in each of the data periods. 170 countries have between 1 and 3 data points, and missing data are estimated by using a model with region, country, and time variables. The model keeps the original observation if data are available for any of the time periods. This modeling approach allowed the estimation of electrification rates for 212 countries over these 3 time periods (indicated as "Estimate"). The notation "Assumption" refers to the assumption of universal access in countries classified as developed by the United Nations. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The classification was confined using a mangrove habitat mask, which defined regions where mangrove ecosystems can be expected to exist. The mangrove habitat definition was based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on a randomly sample of 38 million points using the mangrove masks (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. (2011) and Spalding et al. (2010) and the water occurrence layer defined by Pekel et al. (2017). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Crop Allocation to Food, Feed, Nonfood
description:
### Overview  
  
The Crop Allocation to Food, Feed, Nonfood dataset shows how crops are used around the world. The dataset also shows calorie production per what fraction of global crop production actually becomes food. This data shows how many kilocalories of food, feed, and nonfood are produced by 41 crops combined. Food includes all kilocalories used for human consumption, feed includes those used for animal feed, and nonfood includes those used for biofuels and other industrial uses. Worldwide demand for crops is increasing rapidly due to global population growth, increased biofuel production, and changing dietary preferences. Meeting these growing demands will be a substantial challenge that will tax the capability of the food system and prompt calls to dramatically boost global crop production. However, to increase food availability, we may also consider how the world’s crops are allocated to different uses and whether it is possible to feed more people with current levels of crop production.
 
  
  
This data was developed by researchers at the University of Minnesota. It reflects the production and use of 41 crops combined, circa 2000. The spatial resolution of the data is five arc minutes by five arc minutes (~10 km x 10 km at the equator).
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Crop-specific uses for 41 crops were estimated based on the Food Balance Sheets (FAOstat.org) produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), which provide national-level statistics. This data uses a global compilation of census data and satellite images to depict geographic patterns of crop area and yields across the world on a 5′ × 5′ latitude–longitude grid (equivalent to roughly 9 km × 9 km on the equator). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/8/3/034015/meta).

title: [Archived] Gender Development Index
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](cf069d6d-27b0-4282-8ff3-ee04d90e841d) as a replacement.**_
  
The Gender Development Index (GDI), published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), measures gender gaps in human development achievements by accounting for disparities between women and men in 3 basic dimensions of human development using the same component indicators as in the Human Development Index (HDI). The HDI is a summary measure of average achievement in key dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, being knowledgeable, and a decent standard of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the 3 dimensions. The health dimension is assessed by life expectancy at birth; the education dimension is measured by mean of years of schooling for adults aged 25 years and more and expected years of schooling for children of school-entering age. The standard-of-living dimension is measured by gross national income per capita. The HDI uses the logarithm of income to reflect the diminishing importance of income with increasing gross national income (GNI). The scores for the 3 HDI dimension indices are then aggregated into a composite index using geometric mean. The GDI is the ratio of the HDIs calculated separately for females and males using the same methodology as in the HDI. It is a direct measure of gender gap, showing the female HDI as a percentage of the male HDI. The GDI is calculated for 161 countries in 2015 and shows how much women are lagging behind their male counterparts in each dimension of human development. It facilitates understanding of the real gender gap in human development achievements and is useful in designing policy tools to close the gap. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Chlorophyll Concentration
description:
### Overview  
  
The Chlorophyll Concentration dataset shows global near-real-time concentrations of chlorophyll-a in the ocean. Concentrations are presented in milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3). Chlorophylls are pigments found in photosynthetic plants that transform sunlight into energy. Chlorophyll-a is a certain type of chlorophyll found in green plants and is responsible for their green hues. Chlorophyll-a concentration in the ocean is used as a way of measuring phytoplankton. High concentrations of chlorophyll-a indicate a large amount, or bloom, of phytoplankton. Phytoplankton are small floating plants that form at the surface of the ocean. Chlorophyll-a concentrations were derived from data measured by a remote sensor aboard the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Aqua satellite. Satellite data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km) and averaged at the end of each month. 

  
  
Chlorophyll concentration maps provide valuable information about the health of the oceans and Earth's climate system. They can be used to measure changes in oceanic productivity and model the Earth’s carbon and nitrogen cycles. The near real-time data is particularly useful for tracing oceanographic currents, jets and plumes. Most phytoplankton blooms are a sign of good ocean health, such as the large blooms that occur in the North Atlantic Ocean every spring. As they grow, phytoplankton take in carbon dioxide and produce oxygen, which could have a positive impact on climate change. However, some phytoplankton blooms can grow out of control into harmful algal blooms. As phytoplankton rapidly die and decay, they can rob the ocean of oxygen and create dead zones where fish and other marine organisms cannot survive. 

  
  
The Chlorophyll Concentration dataset is a combination of work from several organizations within [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/). The [Aqua satellite](https://aqua.nasa.gov/) and [Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS)](https://modis.gsfc.nasa.gov/) instrument are managed by [NASA’s Earth Observing System (EOS) Project Science Office](https://eospso.nasa.gov/). Satellite data is processed by [NASA’s Ocean Biology Processing Group (OBPG)](https://oceancolor.gsfc.nasa.gov/) and satellite imagery is generated by [NASA Earth Observations (NEO)](https://neo.sci.gsfc.nasa.gov/). Collectively, these groups work towards improving the understanding of the Earth as a system by providing a picture of climate and environmental changes as they occur.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Chlorophyll Concentration (mg/m3) was derived from ocean color data measured by the MODIS remote-sensing instrument aboard NASA’s Aqua satellite. Launched in 2002, the Aqua satellite views the entire surface of the Earth every two days and continuously measures data in 36 spectral bands. The primary product derived from MODIS measurements is [remote sensing reflectances (Rrs)](https://oceancolor.gsfc.nasa.gov/atbd/rrs/). Rrs is the spectral distribution of reflected visible solar radiation upwelling from below the ocean surface and passing through the boundary between the ocean and the atmosphere . Chlorophyll Concentration was calculated by two algorithms: the standard band ratio algorithm (OC3M) merged with the color index (CI) of [Hu et al. (2012)](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/resolve/doi?DOI=10.1029/2011JC007395). Both algorithms use the empirical relationship derived from in-situ measurements of chlorophyll near the ocean’s surface and MODIS-measured Rrs in the blue-to-green region of the visible color spectrum. The CI algorithm was used for chlorophyll retrievals below 0.15 mg/m3 and the OC3M algorithm was used for chlorophyll retrievals above 0.2 mg/m3. For chlorophyll retrievals between those values, the CI and OC3M algorithm were blended using a weighted approach. Additional information about the chlorophyll-a algorithm can be found [here](https://oceancolor.gsfc.nasa.gov/atbd/chlor_a/). 

  
  
Satellite data was measured daily at a 1 km spatial resolution. The final Chlorophyll Concentration dataset was produced by averaging the processed data each month and remapping cloud-free ocean bins. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: ene.041.rw0 Electricity Exports
Historical Anthropogenic Biomes
description:
### Overview  
  
The History Database of the Global Environment (HYDE version 3.2), is a combination of gridded historical population and land use estimates. The authors used historical records to model population at the province level and land use areas at the national level through time; then used algorithms to spatially distribute the total population and land use areas to 5 arc minute pixels (about 10 kilometers at the equator).
  
  

HYDE is the first spatially explicit estimate of population and land use going back to 10,000 BC. This dataset on Resource Watch describes the land use data of HYDE and the population data can be viewed [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc088a-HYDE-Historical-Population-2).
  
  

Land use is represented in HYDE in two formats. The first representation shows each land use category as fractional coverage per pixel, or how much of the land in that pixel is devoted to each land use category. The second representation has pixels classified as [Anthropogenic Biomes](http://ecotope.org/anthromes/v1/guide/) or “Anthromes” from [Ellis and Ramankutty (2008)](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/070062). 
  
  

Anthropogenic Biomes are globally significant ecological patterns created by sustained interactions between humans and ecosystems.  In a similar way that classic biomes are formed by global patterns of climate, anthromes are formed by global patterns in human populations and their use of land over the long-term. Anthropogenic Biome categories are grouped as urban, dense settlements, villages, croplands, rangelands, semi-natural woodlands, semi-natural areas, and wild. These categories are further subdivided into specific land uses to give greater detail.
  
  

The dataset has global coverage from 10,000 BC to 2017 AD at  a resolution of 5 arc minutes (about 10 km). HYDE was developed by the PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency, and is used by the World Climate Research Program Coupled Model Intercomparison Project ([CMIP6](https://www.wcrp-climate.org/wgcm-cmip/wgcm-cmip6)).   
  
### Methodology  
  
The authors used historical records to model population at the province level and land use areas at the national level through time and then used algorithms to spatially distribute the total population and land use areas to 5 arc minute pixels (about 10 kilometers at the equator).
  
  

For recent country totals of cropland and pasture, the authors used data from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO 2015), who present country totals for cropland and pasture for the post-1960 period. 
  
  

For country totals of cropland and pasture in the pre-1960 period, the authors first estimated land use per capita for each country. This represents how much cropland and pasture area is needed per person. For 1960 onwards the per capita cropland and grazing land was derived from FAO data and then modelled back in time. Modeling was done assuming agricultural land use  was not constant, but instead followed a curved trajectory that is country dependent and based on limited historical references. The historical country totals of cropland and pasture were then calculated by multiplying the estimated per capita rate by the total population from their [population](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc088a-HYDE-Historical-Population-2) dataset.
  
  

Further specific input statistics on cropland and pastureland at a subnational level were used for some of the larger countries in the world, such as the USA (USDA, 2006), Canada (Urquhart and Buckley, 1965), Mexico (World Atlas of Agriculture, 1969), Argentina (Vazquez-Presedo, 1988), Brazil (N. Ramankutty, personal communication, 2001), India (Flint and Richards, 1991; Indiastat, 2009), China (China National Bureau of Statistics, 2008; Ge et al., 2008; He et al., 2012, 2013) and Australia (Australian Bureau of Statistics, 2001). Furthermore, other country-specific sources were used when available for specific information per country. These sources are outlined in the supplementary information of their [methodology](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/9/927/2017/). 
  
  

Once the country totals were determined for cropland and pasture, the authors used allocation algorithms to spatialize the country totals. 
For present day, the authors allocated country totals using the European Space Agency’s Land Cover 2010 consortium map (ESA, 2016; Hollman et al., 2013). The authors used country specific allocation algorithms to distribute country totals from FAO to the most likely ESA land cover categories. 
The authors determined historical distributions of cropland and pasture using population, soil suitability, climate suitability accessibility, and other factors to allocate the country level totals to the pixel level.
  
  

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/9/927/2017/).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows data from the HYDE dataset showing [population density](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc088a-HYDE-Historical-Population-2).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The HYDE dataset has additional data on population count, rural population count, urban population count, and urban built-up area. HYDE provides data on land use including pasture areas, irrigated crops and rainfed crops. The HYDE dataset covers 10,000 BC to 2017 at the following time intervals: every 1000 years from 10,000 BC to 0 AD, every 100 years from 0 AD to 1700 AD, every 10 years from 1700 AD to 2000, and every year from 2000 to 2017. title: Local Threats to Coral Reefs
description:
### Overview  
  
The health of coral reefs is threatened from many nearby human activities. This dataset describes, individually and in aggregate, the threat posed by the following nearby activities: coastal development, marine-based pollution, watershed-based pollution, and overfishing and other destructive fishing practices. This dataset expresses these threats via an index of low, medium, or high threat severity at a 1 km resolution (the integrated threat index also includes a "very high" category).   
  
The dataset was created at the World Resources Institute (WRI) as part of the Reefs at Risk Revisited study and represents threats for the year 2011. The coral reef location dataset used was based on 500 meter resolution gridded data reflecting shallow, tropical coral reefs of the world. Organizations contributing to the data and development of the map include the Institute for Marine Remote Sensing at the University of South Florida (IMaRS USF), Institut de Recherche pour le Développement (IRD), United Nations Environment World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC), WorldFish Center, and WRI.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Local threats to coral reefs include: coastal development; marine-based pollution and damage; watershed-based pollution; and overfishing and destructive fishing practices. To combine these into one index, the authors defined the factors that contribute to each threat in the following way:  
  
The coastal development threat includes the number, size, population density, and population growth rates of human settlements on the coast; locations of seaports, airports and hotels; and traffic from tourism.  
  
The marine-based pollution and damage threat includes datasets on distance from commercial and cruise ports, shipping intensity as measured by a voluntary reporting scheme, and presence of oil infrastructure.   
  
The watershed-based pollution threat to coral reefs includes sediment deposits accumulated throughout watersheds and released at river mouths. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) is used to calculate the relative erosion potential (REP) for all land areas. The REP levels in a watershed are used to determine how much sediment gets loaded into the water courses of the watershed. Factors such as mangroves and dams reduce the total sediment delivery at the river mouth. A model is used to disperse the accumulated sediment amount in the surrounding ocean area. Thresholds are established to differentiate between ocean grid cells at low, medium, or high threat from sediment deposits.  
  
Severity of overfishing was estimated based on proxies for demand for fish products---coastal population density, extent of official fishing areas, and reef and shallow shelf areas---with special adjustments made to account for increased demand when in proximity to large populations and market centers. Areas where destructive fishing practices occur, such as using explosives or poisons, were included based on observations from monitoring and mapping exercises undertaken by field experts.   
  
The overfishing and destructive fishing threat level may be reduced by one level if a grid cell was inside a marine protected area that had been rated as having “effective” or “partially effective” management. These ratings were sourced from regional experts, who were asked to rate marine protected areas on a three-point scale for management effectiveness.   
  
Depending on the size of these threat factors, distance thresholds are established for whether that threat factor puts a nearby ocean grid cell at low, medium, or high risk of damage to coral reefs. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://wriorg.s3.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/pdf/reefs_at_risk_revisited.pdf?_ga=2.65485742.1818236267.1556558259-801875434.1487936749).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for global threats to coral are available from the data provider.  For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Madhya Pradesh Change in Ground Water Recharge
description:
The data displays projected change in the annual ground water recharge from baseline (1981-2010) towards mid-century (2021-2050) in percentage. This data is an output from a hydrologic model, SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) which has been use to assess the impact of projected climate change on water resources. The SWAT model (Arnold et al., 1981, Neitsch et al., 2022) is a distributed parameter and continuous time simulation model. The SWAT model has been developed to predict the hydrological response of un-gauged catchments to natural inputs as well as the manmade interventions. The model (a) is physically based; (b) uses readily available inputs; (c) is computationally efficient to operate and (d) is continuous time and capable of simulating long periods for computing the effects of management changes. The major advantage of the SWAT model is that unlike the other conventional conceptual simulation models it does not require much calibration and therefore can be used on un-gauged watersheds (in fact the usual situation). 

The SWAT model is a long-term, continuous model for watershed simulation. It operates on a daily time step and is designed to predict the impact of land management practices on water, sediment, and agricultural chemical yields. The model is physically based, computationally efficient, and capable of simulating a high level of spatial details by allowing the watershed to be divided into a large number of sub-watersheds. Major model components include weather, hydrology, soil temperature, plant growth, nutrients, pesticides, and land management. The model has been validated for several watersheds.
Input data used are terrain, landuse, soil, daily weather data (rainfall, maximum and minimum temperature, wind speed, relative humidity and wind speed), cropping pattern, reservoirs and any man made structure with their characteristics.

The outputs provided by the model are very exhaustive covering all the components of water balance spatially and temporally. The sub components of the water balance that are more significant and were used for analyses include:

• Precipitation.

• Total flow (Water yield) consisting of surface runoff, lateral and base flow.

• Actual evapotranspiration (Actual ET).

• Base flow.

• Ground water recharge.

title: Aqueduct Coastal Eutrophication Potential
description:
### Overview  
  
Coastal eutrophication potential (CEP) measures the potential for riverine loadings of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and silica (Si) to stimulate harmful algal blooms in coastal waters. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology.  Higher values indicate higher levels of excess nutrients with respect to silica, creating more favorable conditions for harmful algal growth and eutrophication in coastal waters downstream. These risk scores range from low (<-5) to extremely high (>5).

  
  
The CEP indicator is a useful metric to map where anthropogenic activities produce enough point-source and nonpoint-source pollution to potentially degrade the environment. When nitrogen and phosphorus are discharged in excess over silica with respect to diatom, a major type of algae, undesirable algal species often develop. The stimulation of algae leading to large blooms may in turn result in eutrophication and hypoxia (excessive biological growth and decomposition that reduces oxygen available to other organisms). It is therefore possible to assess the potential for coastal eutrophication from a river’s nitrogen, phosphorus, and silica loading. Values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6).
  
  
### Methodology  
  

The calculation described below is based on [Billen and Garnier’s (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marchem.2006.12.017) Indicator of Coastal Eutrophication Potential (ICEP) methodology. The nutrient data comes from [Bouwman et al. (2015)](https://www.thegef.org/project/global-foundations-reducing-nutrient-enrichment-and-odflb-pollution-support-gnc). In short, the data is based on the Global NEWS 2 model [(Mayorga et al. 2010)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2010.01.007) and aligned to Simulated Topological Network basins [(Vörösmarty et al. 2000)](http://dx.doi.org/10.1029/1999GB900092). The NEWS 2 model uses biophysical, natural, and anthropogenic (both point and nonpoint) nutrient sources, along with in-watershed and in-river removal processes, to derive global nutrient yields [(Mayorga et al. 2010)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2010.01.007). Total nitrogen and phosphors fluxes were calculated by summing NEWS 2 nutrient yield data for dissolved organic, dissolved inorganic, and particulate nutrients. Silica fluxes are simply the dissolved inorganic silica yields in the basin.

  
  
The calculation is based on the Redfield molar ratio (C:N:P:Si = 106:16:1:20), which is a representation of the approximate nutrient requirement of marine diatoms [(Billen and Garnier 2007)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marchem.2006.12.017). 

  
  
A negative value indicated that silica was present in excess over the limiting nutrient and thus suggested the absence of eutrophication. A positive value indicated an excess of nutrients over the potential for diatom growth, suggesting suitable conditions for the growth of harmful algae [(Garnier et al. 2010)](https://doi.org/10.1029/2009GB003583).  

  
  
As a final step, the results were aggregated to HydroBASIN level 6 to align the indicator with the remainder of the framework.

  
  
Finally, raw coastal eutrophication potential values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw coastal eutrophication potential values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.
- Low (0-1): < -5
- Low to medium (1-2): -5 - 0
- Medium to high (2-3): 0 - 1
- High (3-4): 1 - 5
- Extremely high (4-5): >5

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology]( https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature U.S. (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average maximum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the maximum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average maximum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average maximum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCAdata on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily maximum temperature data over a given year. The average annual maximum temperatures were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average maximum temperature.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual maximum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Sustainable Energy for All Progress Tracking

These indicators are assembled by a coalition of partner agencies, led by the World Bank, the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP), along with more than 20 other partner agencies. For a full list, see http://gtf.esmap.org/about-us. The 2017 edition of the GTF includes the following indicators on the 3 SE4ALL goals: access to electricity for urban, rural, and total populations; primary energy intensity; and total final energy consumption; the share of renewable energy in total final energy consumption; renewable energy consumption; share of renewable energy in electricity output; total electricity output; and renewable energy electricity output. Each of these indicators has a unique methodology, all of which can be reviewed in the GTF methodology at http://gtf.esmap.org/methodology. title: Aqueduct Baseline Water Stress
description:
### Overview  
  
Baseline water stress measures the ratio of total water withdrawals to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. A higher ratio indicates more competition among users. These ratios were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low water stress (<10%) to extremely high water stress (>80%). Water withdrawals include domestic, industrial, irrigation and livestock consumptive and non-consumptive uses. Available renewable water supplies include surface and groundwater supplies and the impact of upstream consumptive water use and large dams on downstream water availability. Water stress values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6).   
  
### Methodology  
  
Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB
2), to calculate five indicators. Baseline water stress is one of those indicators and was calculated using the gross and net total withdrawal and available water per sub-basin time series from the default model run.   
  
The model was first used to calculate a time series of water stress per catchment per month. To calculate water stress, total withdrawals were divided by the available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Net consumptive water use was subtracted from the total available renewable water supply before the ratio was calculated. The results were output in 12 monthly time series time series of water stress per sub-basin. Water resources in delta sub-basins were pooled.  
  
Next, the time series were converted into baseline values using an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. For example, the regression output for January 2020 represents the chronic, long-term condition of water stress in January’s from 1960 to 2020. This was repeated for every month and then averaged into an annual value.  All raw values were limited to a maximum of 100% and a minimum of 0%.   
  
Sub-basins that were classified “Arid and low water use” were handled separately and were given a raw value for baseline water stress of -1.  
  
Finally, raw baseline water stress values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw baseline water stress values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.  
  
- Low (0-1): < 10%  
  
- Low to medium (1-2): 10-20%  
  
- Medium to high (2-3): 20-40%  
  
- High (3-4): 40-80%  
  
- Extremely high (4-5): >80%  
  
- Arid and low water use (5): -1  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: Historical Cyclone Intensity
description:
### Overview  
  
The Historical Cyclone Intensity dataset estimates the maximum tropical storm intensity experienced at each point around the globe between 1970 and 2009, as indicated by wind speed. Intensity is described via the Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale, meaning each value represents the "strongest" cyclone within each 1 arc minute grid cell during that time.

  
  
Hurricane‐force winds can destroy buildings and fling dangerous debris. However, storm surge and large waves produced by hurricanes pose the greatest threat to life and property along the coast. A storm surge is an abnormal rise of water generated by a storm's winds.The destructive power of storm surge and large battering waves can result in loss of life, buildings destroyed, beach and dune erosion, and road and bridge damage along the coast. Storm surge can span hundreds of miles of coastland and can travel several miles inland. In estuaries and bayous, salt water intrusion endangers public health and the environment. More powerful storms can lead to stronger winds and larger surges. Tracking historical cyclone events can help in estimating the level of threat posed by storms in a given region.

  
  
Observations of historical cyclone events are sparse globally, which led researchers to estimate storm characteristics using [a parametric model created by Greg Holland](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(1980)108%3C1212:AAMOTW%3E2.0.CO;2). These modeled results are based primarily on [IBTrACS](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/ibtracs/) v02r01—the most complete global set of historical tropical cyclones available—but United Nations Environment Programme/Global Resource Information Database-Geneva(UNEP/GRID-Geneva) reconciled a wide range of datasets into a common framework. By applying modeling equations to this unified historical archive, UNEP/GRID-Geneva built a homogeneous structured cyclone database with first level basic
meteorological data and spatial data. This global cyclone database makes possible
post-analysis of historical cyclone events, such as the dataset presented here.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset is derived from a geospatial database of historical tropical storms, which includes estimates of wind speeds and other properties across space and time. This database drew upon [IBTrACS](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/ibtracs/) v02r01 as well as tropical cyclone data from Regional Specialised Meteorological Centres (RSMCs) and the Tropical Cyclone
Warning Centres (TCWCs) of the World Meteorological Organisation. This database was constructed using the [Cyclone Database Manager](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.117.6313&rep=rep1&type=pdf) created by UNEP/DEWA/GRID-Geneva.

  
  
Geospatially complete characterizations of historical tropical storms were extrapolated from historical observations using [a parametric model created by Greg Holland](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(1980)108%3C1212:AAMOTW%3E2.0.CO;2), which was selected on the basis of universal recommendation from all polled tropical cyclone specialists. Data compilation and GIS processing were executed by UNEP/GRID-Europe as part of the production of the [Global Assessment Report on Risk Reduction (GAR)](https://gar.undrr.org/).

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button or see the [source methodology](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.117.6313&rep=rep1&type=pdf) for the underlying cyclone database.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch displays the [IBTrACS historical tropical cyclone tracks](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/dis015a-Hurricane-Tracks) on which this historical intensity dataset is largely based.

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ocn_005_historical_cyclone_intensity).

title: U.S. Hospitals Per 100,000 People
description:
The Heat Vulnerability - Adaptive Capacity: Hospitals per 100,000 people data set was created by the Center for Disease Control and Prevention in order to identify communities at risk and the percentage of possibly vulnerable population in the United States.

Hospital location data was provided by the American Hospital Association (AHA) from 2012. The number of hospitals per county were calculated by determining the location of each hospital, as provided by AHA, and which county each hospital resides, as defined by the TIGER boundary data provided by the US Census Bureau. The rate of hospitals per 100,000 people was calculated using the total population per county, as proved by 2010 US Census data. The rate of hospitals per 100 square miles was calculated using US Census TIGER Boundary data for each county. Blanks or missing data within the maps, tables, and charts may be due to one of the following reasons: (1) data were not collected, (2) data were collected but were not provided to CDC, or (3) data were incomplete or did not meet data quality standards.

title: Dynamic World
description:
The Dynamic World (Land Cover product) dataset shows globally consistent, high resolution, near real-time (NRT) land use land cover (LULC) classification leveraging deep learning on 10 meters Sentinel-2 imagery. The dataset was created utilizing a highly scalable cloud-based system to apply this approach and provide an open, continuous feed of  LULC predictions in parallel with Sentinel-2 acquisitions. The dataset includes the following Land Cover types: water, trees, grass, flooded vegetation, crops, shrub/scrub, built area, bare ground, and snow/ice.  You can learn more about the dataset [here](http://dynamicworld.app).  

Regularly updated global land use land cover (LULC) datasets provide the basis for understanding the status, trends, and pressures of human activity on carbon cycles, biodiversity, and other natural and anthropogenic processes. Annual maps of global LULC have been developed by many groups and while widely used, many important LULC change processes are difficult or impossible to observe at a spatial resolution greater than 100 meters and annual temporal resolution, such as emerging settlements and small-scale agriculture and early stages of deforestation and wetland/grassland conversion. Inability to resolve these processes introduces significant errors in our understanding of ecological dynamics and carbon budgets. Thus, there is a critical need for spatially explicit, moderate resolution (10-30 meters/pixel) LULC products that are updated with greater temporal frequency.  

The Dynamic World dataset is a first-of-its-kind NRT product, which accommodates a variety of user needs ranging from extremely up-to-date LULC data to custom global composites representing user-specified date ranges. Furthermore, the continuous nature of the product's outputs enables refinement, extension, and even redefinition of the LULC classification. In combination, these attributes enable unprecedented flexibility for a diverse community of users across a variety of disciplines. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The classification schema for Dynamic World was determined after a review of global LULC maps. The Dynamic World taxonomy maintains a close semblance to the land use classes presented in the [IPCC Good Practice Guidance](https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/public/gpglulucf/gpglulucf.html) to ensure easier application of the resulting data for estimating carbon stocks and greenhouse gas emissions.   

The modeling approach relies on semi-supervised deep learning and requires spatially dense annotations. To collect a diverse set of training and evaluation data, the authors divided the world into three regions, then further divided each region by the [14 RESOLVE Ecoregions biomes](https://academic.oup.com/bioscience/article/67/6/534/3102935). At each sample location, an initial selection of Sentinel-2 images from 2019 scenes based on image cloudiness metadata reported in the Sentinel-2 tile’s QA60 band was selected. The authors further filtered scenes to remove images with many masked pixels. Individual tiles of 510x510 pixels centered on the sample sites from random dates in 2019 were finally extracted.   

Further steps were then taken to obtain an “as balanced as possible” training dataset with respect to the LULC classifications from the respective LULC products. To achieve a large dataset of labeled Sentinel-2 scenes, the authors worked with two groups of annotators: photo-interpretation experts (validating 4,000 tiles) and non-experts (validating 20,000 tiles). A final validation set of 409 image tiles were held back from the modeling effort and used for evaluation as described in the Technical Validation section of the source methodology. To account for an annotation skill differential between the non-expert and expert groups, they one-hot encode the labeled pixels and smooth them according to the confidence in a binary label of the individual annotator (expert/non-expert).  

For training data collection, the authors used the Sentinel-2 Level-2A (L2A) product, which provides
radiometrically calibrated surface reflectance (SR). However, systematically produced Sentinel-2 SR products are currently only available from 2017 onwards. Therefore, for the modeling approach, the authors used the Level-1C (L1C) product, which was generated from 2015 and represents Top-of-Atmosphere (TOA) reflectance measurements. For any L2A image, there is a corresponding L1C image, allowing them to directly map annotations performed using L2A imagery to the L1C imagery used in model training.  

In addition to their preliminary cloud filtering in training image selection, the authors adopted and applied a novel masking solution that combines several existing products and techniques, including masking cloud shadows.   

The distribution of Sentinel-2 reflectance values is highly compressed towards the low end of the sensor range, with the remainder mostly occupied by high return phenomena like snow and ice, bare ground, and specular reflection. To combat this imbalance, the authors introduce a normalization scheme that better utilizes the useful range of Sentinel-2 reflectance values for each band.  
 
Their broad approach to transferring the supervised label data to a system that could be applied
globally was to train a Fully Convolutional Neural Network (FCNN). Conceptually, this approach transforms pre-processed Sentinel-2 optical bands into a discrete probability distribution of the classes in our taxonomy on the basis of spatial context. This is done per image on the hypothesis that sufficient spatial and spectral context is available to recover one of their taxonomic labels at a pixel. The authors
introduce a number of novel innovations that achieve state-of-the-art performance on LULC globally with a neural network architecture almost 100x smaller than architectures used for semantic segmentation or regression of ground-level camera imagery.  

To generate the NRT products, the authors apply the normalization described earlier to the raw Sentinel-2 L1C imagery and pass all normalized bands except B1, B8A, B9, and B10 after bilinear upscaling to ee.Model.predictImage. This output is then masked using the cloud mask derived from the unnormalized L1C image. The creation of these images is triggered automatically when new Sentinel-2 L1C and S2C images are available.The NRT collection is continuously updated with new results.  

For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Climate - countries available list
Population (Grid, 100m)
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset from WorldPop shows a gridded estimated count of every country’s population. This dataset is shown at a 3 arc second resolution, which is approximately 100 meters at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. This dataset shows constrained population estimates, meaning that population estimates were only generated in areas with built settlements, at an annual timestep from 2000 to 2020.

  
  
Accurate population counts are an essential part of governance, influencing a range of public services and human rights. In application, this data can feed into land zonation, urban planning and public services, and it can be combined with other datasets to create informed disaster risk reduction plans. Population data is used daily to ensure equitable access to services including those that underlie critical democratic processes like voting.

  
  
Population data has historically had a poor temporal resolution, being updated on decadal timeframes. Often these data have been of a spatial resolution that is too low to integrate into many essential fields including policy analysis, scientific development, and operational work. WorldPop aims to provide regular, consistent, high resolution population data through methodological innovation. This data aims to support the measurement of local populations, their characteristics and growth across national and regional scales.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The most accurate current estimates of population come from housing and population censuses, which are often collected as a country per administrative unit. WorldPop generates a gridded version of the dataset through a top-down [constrained estimation modelling method](https://www.worldpop.org/methods/top_down_constrained_vs_unconstrained). The method uses satellite derived building footprint data in combination with a built settlement growth model to account for the distribution of settlements. Random forest-based modelling is then used to disaggregate the population count estimates to the grid cells identified as containing buildings/built settlements.

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.worldpop.org/methods).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Resource Watch visualizes population estimates using the [constrained methodology](https://www.worldpop.org/methods/top_down_constrained_vs_unconstrained); however, the source also offers population estimates under an unconstrained methodology. For additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  

Resource Watch previously showed data on Historical Population Density, which included data between 1975 and 2015. This dataset has been archived. You can still access the archived data [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b6ceb159-efd8-42de-9c6a-d658801d8922).
