title: Forest GHG emissions - 2001-2021 test
Madhya Pradesh Change in Rainfall
description:
The data represents projected change in the annual rainfall from baseline (1981-2010) towards mid-century (2021-2050) in percentage. This data is an output from a hydrologic model, SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) which has been use to assess the impact of projected climate change on water resources. The SWAT model (Arnold et al., 1981, Neitsch et al., 2022) is a distributed parameter and continuous time simulation model. The SWAT model has been developed to predict the hydrological response of un-gauged catchments to natural inputs as well as the manmade interventions. The model (a) is physically based; (b) uses readily available inputs; (c) is computationally efficient to operate and (d) is continuous time and capable of simulating long periods for computing the effects of management changes. The major advantage of the SWAT model is that unlike the other conventional conceptual simulation models it does not require much calibration and therefore can be used on un-gauged watersheds (in fact the usual situation). 

The SWAT model is a long-term, continuous model for watershed simulation. It operates on a daily time step and is designed to predict the impact of land management practices on water, sediment, and agricultural chemical yields. The model is physically based, computationally efficient, and capable of simulating a high level of spatial details by allowing the watershed to be divided into a large number of sub-watersheds. Major model components include weather, hydrology, soil temperature, plant growth, nutrients, pesticides, and land management. The model has been validated for several watersheds.

Input data used are terrain, landuse, soil, daily weather data (rainfall, maximum and minimum temperature, wind speed,, relative humidity and wind speed), cropping pattern, reservoirs and any man made structure with their characteristics.
The outputs provided by the model are very exhaustive covering all the components of water balance spatially and temporally. The sub components of the water balance that are more significant and were used for analyses include:

• Precipitation.

• Total flow (Water yield) consisting of surface runoff, lateral and base flow.

• Actual evapotranspiration (Actual ET).

• Base flow.

• Ground water recharge.

title: [Archived] Current Water Risk
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c66d7f3a-d1a8-488f-af8b-302b0f2c3840) as a replacement.**_
  
In response to growing concerns from private sector actors around water availability, water quality, climate change, and increasing demand, World Resources Institute developed Aqueduct Global Maps to help decision-makers identify areas with higher exposure to water-related risks. Aqueduct employs the composite index approach as a robust communication tool to translate hydrological data into intuitive indicators of water-related risks. 12 indicators were grouped into a framework identifying spatial variation in water risks for 15,006 subcatchments. The 12 global indicators (baseline water stress, interannual variability, seasonal variability, flood occurrence, drought severity, upstream storage, groundwater stress, return flow ratio, upstream protected land, media coverage, access to water, and threatened amphibians) were grouped into 3 categories of risk (physical quantity, quality, and regulatory and reputational risk) and 1 overall score. For 6 of the 12 indicators, an ensemble of time series estimators, spatial regression, and a sparse hydrological model was used to generate novel data sets of water supply and use. The remaining 6 indicators were adapted from existing publications. Aggregation methods were chosen to maximize transparency and communicability, and to allow for dynamic weighting to reflect different users’ sensitivities to water-related risks. Catchments with less than 0.012 m/m²/year of withdrawal and 0.03 m/m²/year of available blue water were masked out as “arid and low water use.” Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Legend Test Dataset
Air Quality: Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Modeled Next-day Forecast
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows forecasted sulfur dioxide (SO₂) concentrations at Earth's surface, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM).   
  
Sulfur dioxide is a colorless, reactive air pollutant with a strong odor. The gas is a respiratory irritant that can harm human health. According to the [Australian Department of Environment and Energy](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-sulfur-dioxide-so2), sulfur dioxide irritates the nose, throat, and airways. It can cause shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, or a tight feeling around the chest. High concentrations of sulfur dioxide can affect lung function, worsen asthma attacks, and worsen existing heart disease in sensitive groups.  
  
Most sulfur dioxide emissions come from the burning of coal, oil or gas for electricity and transportation; these fossil fuels contain sulfur, which is emitted as sulfur dioxide when burned. Sulfur dioxide does not contribute to global warming, but it [reacts easily](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-sulfur-dioxide-so2) with other substances to form harmful compounds such as sulfuric acid and small sulfate particles. When sulfur dioxide reacts with water and oxygen, it [creates acid rain](https://www.epa.gov/acidrain/what-acid-rain). Acid rain has a number of [environmental impacts](https://www.ucsusa.org/clean-energy/coal-and-other-fossil-fuels/hidden-cost-of-fossils), including making lakes, rivers, wetlands and other water bodies more acidic, which can be harmful to fish and other aquatic wildlife.  
  
WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted sulfur dioxide concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO).  WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps.   
  
WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution.  
  
### Methodology  
  
WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere are also produced by WACCM. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_038_waccm_atmospheric_chemistry_model).

Emissions Comparison of Electric and Diesel Buses
description:
The CO₂ Emissions Comparison for Transit Buses was developed by World Resources Institute (WRI) using emission factors for grid electricity from Ecometrica, fuel combustion emissions data from International Energy Agency 2012 and 2013(IEA), electric power transmission and distribution loss data from the World Bank Group's World Development Indicators, and purchased electricity values from Greenhouse Gas Protocol (GHGP).   
  
The climate change impacts of electric vehicles (EV) vary globally depending on the fuel used to power the electric grid. EVs are increasingly becoming a better choice as electric grids improve efficiency and integrate more renewable energy sources. While the efficiency of the vehicle has a large impact on the operational costs, social benefits, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, it is important to understand the energy mix from your local energy grid – as there is significant variation within countries.   
  
The data represents the ratio of CO₂ emissions from electric and diesel buses. The purpose of the data is to compare the GHG emissions of the EV and typical ICE diesel bus for the years 1990-2012 on a national level. Where the interactive Resource Watch global map is green, the emissions from the EV are lower, based on the national average energy grid, compared to the emissions from the typical ICE diesel bus. Where the interactive Resource Watch global map is red, the emissions from the EV are higher, based on the national average energy grid, compared to the emissions from the typical ICE diesel bus.

title: Costa Rica Current Coffee Suitability
description:
This data set shows current coffee suitability. It was created using multiple environmental variables as part of a study that attempts to utilize data from four Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPPC) emissions scenarios to determine the impact of climate change on coffee cultivation in coffee growing regions of Costa Rica. The study was done using georeferenced points obtained from Instituto del Café de Costa Rica (ICAFE), and using the MaxEnt model to simulate the adaptability of coffee production. 

Environmental layers taken into account comprise 19 bioclimatic variables from the Worldclim database. Developed by Hijmans et al. 2005, thousands of data points from meteorological stations around the world were collected for the time period of 1960 to 1990, using an interpolation to create environmental layers (rasters) of average temperature with 24,542 locations, minimum and maximum temperatures with 14,835 locations, and precipitation with 47,554 locations. These were all calculated by month, with a resolution of 1 square km. Bioclimatic variables were derived from monthly temperature and precipitation values with the goal of generating biologically significant variables related to crop development.

title: [Archived] Terrestrial Ecoregions
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](d0968f74-f5c1-40a1-b2b5-5bac5de5cb15) as a replacement.**_
  
The Terrestrial Ecoregions data set released by The Nature Conservancy (TNC), and updated in 2008 from compilations of previous studies, classifies land into 14 major habitat types (MHTs). MHTs reflect groupings of ecoregions with similar biological, chemical, and physical characteristics. The MHTs refer to the dynamics of ecological systems and the broad habitat structures that define them. These groupings can provide a structured framework for examining and comparing the diversity of life in terrestrial systems.   
  
MHTs are broadly broken down by latitude, ranging from boreal and tundra, temperature, and tropical regions. Temperate and tropical forests are further broken down into broadleaf and conifers. These regions are also distinguished by moisture level, ranging from desert, xeric, and dry, to moist habitats. Finally, shrublands are distinguished by elevation, from high altitude montane shrublands to flooded lowlands. The ecoregions, originally developed by Olson and Dinerstein (2002), Bailey (1995), and Environment Canada (Wiken 1986), were modified by TNC. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Land Cover
description:
The Climate Change Initiative (CCI) Land Cover (LC) project of the European Space Agency (ESA) delivers consistent global LC maps at 300 m spatial resolution on an annual basis from 1992 to 2015. Each pixel value corresponds to the label of a land cover class defined based on the UN Land Cover Classification System (LCCS). This unique data set was produced thanks to the reprocessing and the interpretation of 5 different satellite missions. Baseline LC maps are generated thanks to the entire MERIS FR and RR archive from 2003 through 2012. Independently from this baseline, LC changes are detected at 1 km based on the AVHRR time series between 1992 to 1999, SPOT-VGT time series between 1999 and 2013, and PROBA-V data for years 2013, 2014, and 2015. When MERIS FR or PROBA-V time series are available, changes detected at 1 km are remapped at 300 m. The last step consists in back- and updating the 10-year baseline LC map to produce the 24 annual LC maps from 1992 to 2015. 

The resulting data have a total of 22 global land cover classes. For the sake of better visualization, PREPdata shows only a set of simplified classes, based on the IPCC (agriculture, forest, grassland, wetland, settlement, shrubland, sparse vegetation, bare area, water, and permanent ice and snow).

title: Areas Vulnerable to Coastal Flooding & Sea Level Rise (m)
description:
The Areas Vulnerable to Coastal Flooding and Sea-Level Rise data set is prepared by Climate Central. These layers are relative to local high tide lines (mean higher high water, or MHHW). Map areas below the selected water level are displayed in blue, indicating vulnerability to flooding from combined sea-level rise, storm surge, and tides, or to permanent submergence by long-term sea-level rise. Elevation data used for parts of this map within the United States come almost entirely from ~5 m horizontal resolution digital elevation models curated and distributed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in its Coastal Lidar collection, derived from high-accuracy laser-rangefinding measurements. Areas outside the United States use elevation data on a roughly 90 m horizontal resolution grid derived from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM). Local high tide level is determined using 2 data sources as well: the VDatum tidal model for the contiguous United States and a global tidal model supplied by Mark Merrifield of the University of Hawaii for the rest of the world.

title: U.S. Hurricane Strikes
description:
NOAA aims to provide tropical cyclone best track data in a centralized location to aid our understanding of the distribution, frequency, and intensity of tropical cyclones worldwide. These data are derived from the NOAA National Weather Service revised Atlantic hurricane database (HURDAT2) data set and the NOAA National Climatic Data Center’s International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS) data set. Storms from 1842 to the present for the United States Atlantic coast are available. Data aquisition tools were developed as part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Office for Coastal Management's Historical Hurricanes Tool, but contain data and information from a variety of data sources, including non-NOAA data.

The strike data includes both direct and indirect hits.  When the innermost core regions, or "eye," moved over a county, it was counted as a direct hit. "R" is defined as the radius of maximum winds in a hurricane (the distance in miles from the storm's center to the circle of maximum winds around the center). A county is regarded as receiving a direct hit when all or parts of a county fall within about 2R to the right and R to the left of a storm's landfall. This assumes an observer at sea looking toward shore. On average, this direct hit zone extended about 50 miles along the coastline (Rz15 miles). Of course, some hurricanes were smaller than this and some, particularly in higher latitudes, were much larger. Indirect hits are characterized by the hurricane's strength and size and on the configuration of the individual county coastline. Here, much subjectivity was necessary, often complicated by storm paths and geography. Indirect hits include those areas on either side of the direct hit zone which received hurricane force winds or tides of at least 4 to 5 feet above normal. Cases were judged individually, and many borderline situations had to be resolved. In effect, this data is useful for making general comparisons between counties, but may not represent an exact, objective count.

title: Trees in Mosaic Landscapes
description:
### Overview    
  
The trees in mosaic landscapes (TML) data maps tree extent at the ten-meter scale and enables accurate monitoring of trees in urban areas, agricultural lands, and in open canopy and dry forest ecosystems. The data extent covers 1.4 billion hectares of mosaic landscapes in Latin America and Africa. Mosaic landscapes are defined as regions that can support a wide variety of tree distributions, including sparse tree cover, scattered or clustered open canopy forests, and fragmented closed-canopy forests. 
The data is derived from multi-temporal convolutional neural network models applied to Sentinel optical and radar imagery. Each pixel demarcates the presence of one or more trees with canopy diameters larger than 3 meters and height greater than 5 meters. The value for each pixel represents the sigmoidal probability of detecting a tree , and can be converted to tree cover by averaging the values within a desired window size (e.g. 30 x 30 meter or half-hectare). The data relies on 3 cloud-free observations for 2020 (<97.5% average cloud cover) and less than 1% of the processing area is missing due to the lack of cloud-free observations. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data is generated by analyzing monthly cloud-free mosaics of Sentinel-2 optical imagery and Sentinel-1 radar imagery. We utilize the 10- and 20-meter bottom-of-atmosphere (L2A) bands from Sentinel-2 and the co-polarized vertical transmit/vertical receive (VV) and cross-polarized vertical transmit/horizontal receive (VH) imagery from Sentinel-1. The model used is a modified U-Net convolutional neural network with a temporal gated recurrent unit (GRU) encoder. The methodology is derived from [Brandt and Stolle (2020)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01431161.2020.1841324) with additional improvements to be detailed in a forthcoming paper. Code and model specifics can be accessed on the project [GitHub page](https://github.com/wri/sentinel-tree-cover).

description:
### Overview  
  
The Global Human Settlement (GHS) built-up dataset provides a global estimation of built-up area between 1975 and 2014. It is available for four time periods: 1975, 1975-1990, 1990-2000, and 2000-2014. Built-up areas represent any urbanized regions containing man-made structures, like buildings. The dataset is based on Landsat imaging and analyzed using a model. The data is available at 30 m, 250 m and 1 km resolution in the source dataset. The 30 m version of the data is displayed here. 
  
  
GHS built-up dataset was released by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (EC JRC). This dataset provides an insight into the human presence on Earth. It is important to understand the pattern of cities' growth. It is projected that 68% of the world’s population will live in urban areas by 2050. This information can help governments create more sustainable urbanization policies and have a more long-term plan for urban growth in the future.  
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The data was produced by processing 33,202 satellite images using the Symbolic Machine Learning (SML) method. Each year corresponded to a different source of Landsat data, GLS 1975, GLS 1990, GLS 2000, and ad hoc Landsat 8 collection 2013/2014. The image data records collected by different satellite sensors between 1975 and 2014 were classified and automatically selected if they corresponded to a built-up structure. The information was analyzed using the GHS built-up model. The model utilized algorithms to extract patterns and determine the spatial size of the building surface area. It analyzed knowledge from large amounts of spatial data, and the availability of open and free image data input, to identify areas of the planet with high densities of built-up areas. This dataset was an improved version from the 2015 GHS built-up dataset. It used an improved image processing workflow that allowed for the detection of more built-up areas and reduced the amount of false identifications of built-up areas in the final classification. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://ghsl.jrc.ec.europa.eu/data.php).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for water surface and land with no built-up in any epoch are also available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

Erosion Risk
description:
This layer shows the risk of erosion around the world, from low to high. Erosion and sedimentation by water involves the process of detachment, transport, and deposition of soil particles, driven by forces from raindrops and water flowing over the land surface. Because soil erosion is difficult to measure at large scales, soil erosion models are crucial estimation tools to extrapolate limited data to other localities and conditions. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE), which predicts annual soil loss from rainfall and runoff, is the most common model used at large spatial scales due to its relatively simple structure and empirical basis. The model takes into account rainfall erosivity, topography, soil erodibility, land cover and management, and conservation practices. Because the RUSLE model was developed based on agricultural plot scale and parameterized for environmental conditions in the USA, modifications of the methods and data inputs are necessary to make the equation applicable to the globe. We estimated erosion potential based on the RUSLE model, adjusted to extend its applicability to a global scale. Conservation practices and topography information were not included in this model to calculate global erosion potential, due to data limitation and their relatively minor contribution to the variation in soil erosion at the continental to global scale compared to other factors. The result of the global model was categorized into five quantiles, corresponding to low to high erosion risks.

title: [Archived] Crop Land Area and Production
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](54af072c-7bb5-4bb1-af84-ea7ba0b4fc22) as a replacement.**_
  
### Overview  
  
The Crop Land and Production dataset shows global harvested area and production for four major crops: wheat, soybean, rice and maize. The dataset was derived from the 2005 Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM). The SPAM model aimed to disaggregate (downscale) national and subnational crop statistics using a variety of inputs, such as cropland surface, location of irrigated areas, crop suitability and potential yields, rural population densities, production systems characteristics and crop prices. Crop data was downscaled to a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes. This spatial resolution is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. 

  
  
Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels and increased biofuel demand. Increased demand for these resources will significantly affect land and resource use, climate change, political agendas and technological developments. A comprehensive understanding of the current spatial distribution of the world’s crops is necessary in order to preemptively address these effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset can be used to understand the extent and productivity of key global crops, which will help address food crop demand and its effects. 

  
  
The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was generated by the [Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research Program on Policies, Institutions, and Markets (CGIAR-PIM)](https://pim.cgiar.org/about/). CGIAR-PIM provides support for policies that help farmers improve their lives, produce nutritious and affordable foods, and protect the soil, water and biodiversity in rural landscapes. The program is led by the [International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)](https://www.ifpri.org/about), a CGIAR-PIM research center. IFPRI provides research-based policy solutions to sustainably reduce poverty and end hunger in developing countries. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was part of the larger SPAM dataset, which was developed for the HarvestChoice research initiative. Conducted by IFPRI, [HarvestChoice](https://www.ifpri.org/project/harvestchoice) generated knowledge products to help guide strategic investments to improve the well-being of poor people in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia through more productive and profitable farming.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Crop Land Area and Production dataset shows production and harvested area for global wheat, soybean, rice and maize crops. Production and harvested area were derived from crop physical area generated by the SPAM mathematical model. The SPAM model outputs were distinguished by crop production system. This was done to account for differences in resource use (i.e., type and quantity of seeds, water, labor, machinery, fertilizer and pesticides). Industrialized farming is considered to be high input and uses large amounts of outside resources. Low input and subsistence farming typically use resources directly from the farm (i.e., manure and cover crops) for crop management. The four production systems were defined by water and management type:
- Irrigated – high input (I)
- Rainfed – high input (H)
- Rainfed – low input (L)
- Rainfed – subsistence (S)

  
  
The primary inputs for the SPAM were crop harvested area, production and yield statistics. This data was collected at the smallest available administrative level (i.e., region, district). Crop statistics at the national level were provided by the [United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAOSTAT)](http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#home). Subnational statistics were drawn from these additional FAO datasets:  
- [the global information system on water and agriculture (AQUASTAT)](http://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/)
- [AgroMaps](http://www.fao.org/land-water/land/land-governance/land-resources-planning-toolbox/category/details/en/c/1026341/) 
- [CountrySTAT](http://www.fao.org/in-action/countrystat/en/)
  
  
Subnational crop data was also provided by the global dataset of [monthly irrigated and rainfed crop areas around the year 2000 (MIRCA2000)](https://www.uni-frankfurt.de/45218023/MIRCA), country statistics offices, published literature and expert judgments. The national and subnational crop production statistics were then allocated to 5 arc minute pixels via a cross-entropy optimization model. The cross-entropy approach quantifies the difference between two probability models and was used to minimize modeling uncertainty. The output of this model were pre-allocated physical areas for each crop and production system. 

  
  
The SPAM model used additional biological and economic inputs to allocate the statistics within each pixel. Input data included:
- Cropland extent: Satellite imagery was used to distinguish cropland from other land types (forest, grassland, waterbodies) and delineate the geographic extent within which crop production could be allocated. Satellite imagery was provided by the [International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA-IFPRI) cropland map](https://iiasa.ac.at/web/home/research/ResearchPartners/IFPRI.en.html). The satellite imagery was upscaled from a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds to fit the 5 arc minute resolution of the SPAM model.
- Crop suitability: Crop suitability measured whether cropland met the specific temperature, moisture and soil requirements of each crop. Areas were categorized as very suitable, suitable, moderately suitable and marginally suitable using data from the [Global Agro-Ecological Zones (GAEZV3.0) dataset](https://webarchive.iiasa.ac.at/Research/LUC/GAEZ/index.htm). 
- Irrigated areas: Locations of areas equipped for irrigation from the [FAO’s Global Map of Irrigated Areas (GMIA 5.0)](http://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/geospatial-information/global-maps-irrigated-areas) were used to further refine production system and cropland definitions. 
- Crop prices: Crop prices were used to understand the location and extent of crops, based on the assumption that farmers choose to grow crops that generate the highest revenue. Crop prices were based on FAOSTAT Gross Production Value data from 2004-2006. 
- Market accessibility: Rural population density was used as a proxy for market accessibility, a factor that affects a farmer’s decision to plant a crop. Population density from the [Global Rural and Urban Mapping Project, Version 1 (GRUMPv1)](https://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/collection/grump-v1) was used to classify pixels as rural or urban at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds. This data was aggregated and reclassified to the 5 arc minute pixel resolution of the SPAM model.
- Potential yield: Crop yield is the amount of crop grown per area of land. Potential crop yield information was derived from GAEZ data and used to further direct the allocation optimization process. 
- Cropping intensity and multiple crops: The cropping intensity parameter accounted for the fact that more than one crop can be grown simultaneously on a plot and that crops can be rotated throughout the year. 

  
  
The SPAM model allocated the crops within each administrative unit with pre-allocated crop statistics within a country using an iterative cross-entropy optimization approach in the [General Algebraic Modeling Software (GAMS)](https://www.gams.com/). The model worked by iteratively minimizing the error between the pre-allocated shares of physical area and the allocated shares of physical area in each pixel. 

  
  
Harvested area and production were calculated from crop physical area in each pixel. Physical area was converted to harvested area using the cropping intensity variable. Total harvested area of each crop in each pixel was calculated by summing estimates across the four production systems. Production was calculated by multiplying harvested area with yield (the amount of production per harvested area in kilograms/hectare). Total production was the sum of production from all of a crop’s production systems and was reported in metric tons. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the [SPAM 2005 Technical Documentation](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/DHXBJX).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Spatially-Disaggregated Crop Production Statistics Data for 2005 Version 3.2 has data for 38 other crops (42 total). The full dataset also includes physical area, yield and value of production for all 42 crops. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch.

title: Annual Renewable Energy Capacity
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows national-level electricity generation capacity from renewable energy technologies between 2000 and 2019. Renewable energy capacity measures the maximum amount of electricity that could instantaneously be produced by the existing renewable energy sources within a country. Renewable energy is defined as energy that comes from natural resources that are continually restored. In this dataset, renewable energy sources include wind, solar, hydropower, biofuels, municipal waste, biogas, geothermal, and marine energy. 
  
  

Transitioning to renewable energy technologies can be beneficial to the economy and human health, as well as help reduce climate change. Electricity generation is one of the largest [sources of greenhouse gas emissions](https://www.epa.gov/ghgemissions/sources-greenhouse-gas-emissions), directly contributing to climate change. Transitioning to renewable energy technologies can help reduce our greenhouse gas emissions and be part of the solution to addressing climate change. Renewable energy production also produces less air pollution, which is linked to a number of health concerns, than most fossil fuel energy sources. Furthermore, these technologies provide a reliable source of energy and help diversify energy portfolios, reducing the potential of energy scarcity. 
  
  

This dataset was produced by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) and is updated annually.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data has been obtained from a variety of sources, including an IRENA questionnaire, official national statistics, industry association reports, other reports and news articles.
  
  

Renewable power generation capacity is measured as the maximum net generating capacity of power plants and other installations that use renewable energy sources to produce electricity. For most countries and technologies, the data reflects the capacity installed and connected at the end of the calendar year. 
  
  

For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information

title: Forest Greenhouse Gas Net Flux
description:
### Overview  
  
Net forest carbon flux represents the net exchange of carbon between forests and the atmosphere between 2001 and 2020, calculated as the balance between carbon emitted by forests and removed by (or sequestered by) forests during the model period (megagrams CO2e ha-1). Net carbon flux is calculated by subtracting average annual gross removals from average annual gross emissions in each modeled pixel; negative values are where forests were net sinks of carbon and positive values are where forests were net sources of carbon between 2001 and 2020. Net fluxes are calculated following IPCC Guidelines for national greenhouse gas inventories in each pixel where forests existed in 2000 or were established between 2000 and 2012 according to the Global Forest Change tree cover change data of Hansen et al. (2013). This layer reflects the cumulative net flux during the model period (2001-2020) and must be divided by 19 to obtain average annual net flux; net flux values cannot be assigned to individual years of the model.  
  
  

This net flux layer is part of the forest carbon flux model described in Harris et al. (2021). This paper introduces a geospatial monitoring framework for estimating global forest carbon fluxes which can assist governments and non-government actors with tracking greenhouse gas fluxes from forests and decreasing emissions or increasing removals by forests. All input layers were resampled to a common resolution of 0.00025 x 0.00025 degrees each to match Hansen et al. (2013).  
  
  

Net flux is available for download in two different area units over the model duration: 1) megagrams of CO2e ha-1, and 2) megagrams of CO2e pixel-1. The first is appropriate for visualizing (mapping) net flux because it represent the density of carbon fluxes per hectare. The second is appropriate for calculating the net flux in an area of interest (AOI) because the values of the pixels in the AOI can be summed to obtain the total carbon flux for that area. The values in the latter were calculated by adjusting the net flux per hectare by the size of each pixel, which varies by latitude. When estimating net flux occurring over a defined number of years between 2001 and 2020, divide the provided values by the model duration and then multiply by the number of years in the period of interest.

title: Climate Hazard Indicators (Annual maximum temperatures - mean) Historical and SSP scenarios - Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
description:
### Overview
 
 
The dataset includes five major climatic indicators viz. annual values for minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), total precipitation (mm/year), and the number of rainy days (represented as integers) for two Indian states, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. It features decadal averages from 2020-2100 for Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), including SSP5-8.5, which reflects a high emissions scenario, and SSP2-4.5, representing moderate challenges to both mitigation and adaptation. Additionally, the dataset provides historical data for all the five indicators averaged over the period from 2005 to 2014.
 
 
### Methodology
 
 
**Pre-Processing**: The decadal time periods were labeled as follows: 2020-2029 as 2020, 2030-2039 as 2030, 2040-2049 as 2040, 2050-2059 as 2050, 2060-2069 as 2060, 2070-2079 as 2070, 2080-2089 as 2080, and 2090-2099 as 2090.
 
 
**Layers of interest**: Annual averages of minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), Annual total precipitation (mm/year), and the annual total number of rainy days (represented as integers).
 
 
**Data**: The ERA5 reanalysis dataset (ECMWF 2022), a satellite data product of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts with a spatial resolution of 31 kilometers (km), is used as a reference dataset. The ensemble of downscaled daily time series outputs from global climate models (GCMs). These time series include the historical years covered by the observation time series as well as the specified future years of interest. We have used the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 product, which includes outputs from 34 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models at approximately 25 km spatial resolution.
 
 
### Estimation Methods
 
 
Out of the 35 models, we select the top 3 climate models that perform best for a specific weather variable in a particular geographic region, and present the ensemble mean of these models. The ERA5 dataset is used as a reference, and the comparison is made for the historical period between 1980 and 2014. After selecting the models, we apply a calibration/bias correction procedure to the future time series of the models. This involves aligning the model's frequency distribution with the historical data by shifting the percentiles of the model's distribution. For instance, if the 20th percentile of the model data corresponds to the 30th percentile of the observations, then the 30th percentile of the calibrated model data will match the 20th percentile of the uncalibrated model data.
 
 
For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at Wong, T., and P Switzer. 2023. 'Estimating future local climate hazard probabilities.' Technical Note. Washington, DC: World Resources Institute. Available online at: doi.org/10.46830/writn.22.00074.v2.
 
 
### Description of the Layers
 
 
**Annual Maximum Temperature (℃)**: The daily maximum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average maximum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years.
 
 
**Annual Minimum Temperature (℃)**: The daily minimum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average minimum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years.
 
 
**Annual Mean Temperature (℃)**: The daily mean temperature is calculated by averaging the daily minimum and maximum temperatures. The annual mean temperature is obtained by averaging the daily mean temperatures over the course of a year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years.
 
 
**Annual Total Precipitation (mm/year)**: The daily precipitation values are summed over the entire year to calculate the annual total precipitation. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years.
 
 
**Annual Rainy Days (represented as integers)**: A rainy day is defined as a day with precipitation exceeding 2.5 mm (as per the India Meteorological Department). The total number of rainy days in a year is calculated by summing the rainy days throughout the year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years.
 
 
### Visualizing the Data
 
 
The data is provided at a 25-km resolution and is presented as a raster with a time slider with a separate layer for each variable. The values are visualized using a gradient based on the selected year in the slider, ranging from lighter shade (indicating low values) to darker shade (representing higher values).
 
 
### Disclaimer

title: U.S. Drought Monitor
description:
The U.S. Drought Monitor, established in 1999, is a weekly map of drought conditions produced jointly by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. The U.S. Drought Monitor website is hosted and maintained by the drought center.

The weekly maps are released at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Standard Time each Thursday and are assessments of past conditions based on data through 7 a.m. Eastern time (8 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time) the preceding Tuesday. The map is based on measurements of climatic, hydrologic and soil conditions as well as reported impacts and observations from more than 350 contributors around the country. Eleven climatologists from the partner organizations take turns serving as the lead author each week. The authors examine all the data and use their best judgment to reconcile any differences among sources.

title: Global Peatlands (DEPRECATED)
Seychelles Geologic Events
description:
This dataset displays a set of geologic events on the Seychellois island of Mahé from 1862 through 2011. An assessment of area-specific risk for landslides, flooding, and rockfalls was conducted in 2011 as part of the Sustainable Land Management (SLM) project. The SLM report, Compilation of Information in View of Developing a Geological Risk Map of the Islands of Mahé, Praslin, and La Digue, was shared with the researchers by the Seychellois Department of Risk and Disaster Management and provided the underlying data of this map. Historical data including the event type, date, location, and cause of each geologic event was extracted from the report to create these data points. 
As defined in the source document, landslides are the downslope movement of soil, rock, and organic materials under the effects of gravity. Landslides depicted in this layer represent mass movements in which the material on a zone of weakness is separated from the more stable underlying material. 

Rockfalls are sudden and rapid processes by which a rock detaches from a slope and descends by falling, bouncing, or rolling. They typically occur along cliffs or steep slopes and result in the displacement of large rocks, sometimes landing on roads or built structures. Rockfalls are strongly influenced by gravity, mechanical weathering, and interstitial weather such as regular intervals of rain. 

Debris falls are the processes by which a combination of soil, rock, mud, and organic material detaches from a steep slope and descends by falling, bouncing, or rolling as a conglomerate. They typically occur suddenly along cliffs or steep slopes, resulting in displaced materials that can land on roads or built structures. Debris falls are strongly influenced by gravity, mechanical weathering, and interstitial weather such as regular intervals of rain. 
Debris flow (commonly called a mudslide) is the process by which masses of loose soil, fragmented rocks, mud, organic matter, and water moves down a slope under the influence of gravity. While a debris flow mobilizes as a conglomerate, the components move independently. Source areas of debris flows are typically adorned with steep gullies. Debris flows deposit materials in fan-like shapes at the foot of the slope or accumulate where an obstruction - like a built structure - is encountered. Debris flows are commonly caused by intense surface water flow due to heavy rain that erodes material on a slope.

Slope failures are abrupt processes in which a very steep slope collapses due to weakened self-retainability, or the ability to uphold materials. Slope failures typically occur along slopes that are steeper than landslides and are characterized by smaller-scale movement than landslides. Materials displaced as a result of slope failure accumulate at the bottom of the slope. Slope failures are commonly triggered by heavy rain or earthquakes.

Protected Areas
description:
The World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) is the most comprehensive global spatial data set on marine and terrestrial protected areas available. Protected area data are provided via Protected Planet, the online interface for the WDPA. The WDPA is a joint initiative of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) to compile spatially referenced information about protected areas. The data are provided as shapefiles and updated monthly. Not all protected areas receive the same degree of protection. While some have strict guidelines designed to preserve intact ecosystems, others allow for sustainable land use, often including limited resource extraction. In addition, not all countries use the same terminology when designating a protected area. Universal management categories are designated by the IUCN that stipulate the level of protection for most protected areas. These categories are defined as follows: (Ia) Strict Nature Reserves: protected areas designed to preserve biodiversity and all geological features. Limited human use (e.g., scientific study, education) is allowed and carefully monitored. Strict nature reserves are often used to understand the impact of indirect human disturbance (e.g., burning fossil fuels) because of the area’s high level of preservation. (Ib) Wilderness Areas: protected areas managed to preserve ecosystem processes with limited human use. Wilderness areas cannot contain modern infrastructure (e.g., a visitor’s center), but they allow for local indigenous groups to maintain subsistence lifestyles. These areas are often established to restore disturbed environments. (II) National Parks: protected areas designed to preserve large-scale ecosystems and support human visitation. With conservation as a priority, these areas allow infrastructure and contribute to the local economy by providing opportunities for environmental educational and recreation. (III) National Monuments or Features: areas established to protect a specific natural feature (e.g., cave, grove) or human-made monument with significant historical, spiritual, or environmental importance and the immediate surroundings. Accordingly, natural monuments or features are typically smaller in area and have high human impact resulting from visitor traffic. (IV) Habitat and Species Management Areas: areas designed to conserve specific wildlife populations and/or habitats. Habitat and species management areas often exist within a larger ecosystem or protected area and are carefully managed (e.g., through hunting abatement or habitat restoration) to conserve a target species or habitat. (V) Protected Landscapes and Seascapes: protected areas with ecological, biological, or cultural importance that have been shaped by human use of the landscape. Protected landscapes and seascapes typically cover entire bodies of land or ocean and allow for a number of for-profit activities (e.g., ecotourism) in accordance with the region’s management plan. (VI) Protected Areas with Sustainable Use of Natural Resources: areas designed to manage natural resources and uphold the livelihoods of surrounding communities. These regions have a low level of human occupation, small-scale developments (i.e., not industrial), and part of the landscape in its natural condition.

Cost of Sustainable Water Management
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset represents the cost of action to deliver sustainable water management as outlined in the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 6(SDG6). The datasets presented on Resource Watch encompass the water challenges within SDG6 and show the cost percentage each category requires out of the total cost to achieve sustainable water management. Total Estimated Cost is the annual cost in 2015 USD to deliver on each aspect of sustainable water management, calculated for each country as the cost of action required to close the gap between current and desired conditions.

  
  
This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) to provide a visual representation of the cost to achieve sustainable water management. Water related issues are already a serious concern and will only worsen given the combined effects of population growth, economic growth, and climate change. SDG6 works to “ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all” by 2030. Sustainable water management includes access to drinking water, access to sanitation services, water pollution, water scarcity, and water management. Each of these categories has specific "estimated cost"  and its percentage of the "total estimated cost" can communicate the relative magnitude of the issue, from a financial perspective. This cost does not fully account for the social and economic benefits of resolving each water challenge and should not be used to inform local policy decisions.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset calculates the cost of action to close the gap between current and desired sustainable water management conditions by 2030. Where possible, the calculation method builds off of existing research and methods rather than developing new approaches to calculating the cost of action. The dataset shows values for the total estimated cost to deliver drinking water, deliver access to sanitation services, eliminate industrial water pollution, eliminate agricultural water pollution, address water scarcity, and address water resource management. Each of these categories was created using the formula below:
  
  
Total Estimated Cost = Projected Gap x Solution Cost
                                                                                                                                                    
  
The projected gap is the gap between current and desired conditions. The solution cost is the cost, in 2015 US dollars, that it will take to change each unit of the current condition to the desired condition for the population in 2030. 

  
  
Water management is a quantity that is based on population, so to determine the amount of water required for the population in 2030 estimated population data was taken from 2030 gridded population data in Downscaling Drivers of Global Environmental Change: Enabling Use of Global SRES Scenarios at the National and Grid Levels (Hutton and Varughese 2016). Values for the solution cost of creating access to drinking water and sanitation were taken from the World Bank for 140 low-income countries and estimated for all other countries. Solution costs for industrial water pollution were taken from Hutton and Varughese 2016, for agricultural water pollution from a combination of eight academic articles, and for water scarcity from 2030 Water Resources Group (WRG) reports. The proposed method was designed to be reproducible with data at any scale, however this dataset has been developed using global, comparable data. For full discussion of the calculation method, see the Achieving Abundance Technical Appendix.

  
  
The final datasets were presented as the percentage of costs to achieve each individual form of water management out of the total cost of water management by 2030. The datasets were projected on a global map at a national resolution using vector format. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/resources/data-sets/achieving-abundance).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
The percentage of the total estimated cost to address water resources management is 17% for each country, but this indicator was not shown on Resource Watch map. Please click on the “Table” button in the “Customize Visualization” section to find this data on Resource Watch.  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/wat_064_cost_of_sustainable_water_management).

title: Extreme Heat Days
description:
Extreme heat days represent the annual average count of days with heat greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP).

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Satellite Measurements
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: NO₂ Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) density in the troposphere. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of NO₂ between Earth’s surface and the top of the troposphere. The NO₂ density is reported with units of moles of NO₂ per square meter of air (mol/m²).

  
  
Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is one of the most common compounds in the nitrogen oxides (NOx) group. Other nitrogen oxides include nitric acid (HNO₃) and nitric oxide (NO). NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides, meaning if NO₂ is present it is likely other nitrogen oxides are as well. NO₂ is primarily created by the burning of fuel, which can be from cars, trucks and buses, power plants, and off-road equipment. Breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the human respiratory system. Acute exposures can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms, like coughing, wheezing or difficulty breathing. Longer chronic exposures to elevated concentrations of NO₂ may contribute to the development of asthma and potentially increase susceptibility to respiratory infections. People with asthma, as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂.

  
  
The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system. The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to  provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as NO₂, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The TROPOMI NO₂ dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. The data was retrieved and analyzed using a 3 step process. 

  
  
1. Total NO₂ slant column density was determined from radiance and irradiance spectra measured by TROPOMI. It was analyzed using a Differential Optical Absorption Spectroscopy (DOAS) method. NO₂ slant column density is the amount of NO₂ found along an average path taken by photons traveling from the sun to the satellite sensor.

  
  
2. Slant column density data was then separated into stratospheric and tropospheric categories based on information coming from the satellite’s data assimilation system. Stratospheric data was then removed from the dataset.

  
  
3. Tropospheric slant column density was converted into tropospheric vertical column density and the average NO₂ density for the entire vertical column was calculated. This was determined by applying an appropriate air mass factor (AMF) and actual, daily information on the vertical distribution of NO₂ calculated by the TM5-MP global chemistry transport model. The altitude-dependent AMF used depended on the satellite geometry, terrain height, cloud fraction and height, and surface albedo.

  
  
The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Total Column”.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI).
  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_035_tropomi_atmospheric_chemistry_model).

The Global Roads Inventory Project (GRIP) dataset was developed to provide a more recent and consistent global roads dataset for use in global environmental and biodiversity assessment models. 
 The GRIP dataset is mainly aimed at providing a roads dataset that is easily usable for scientific global environmental and biodiversity modelling projects. The dataset is not suitable for navigation. GRIP4 is based on many different sources (including OpenStreetMap) and to the best of our ability we have verified their public availability, as a criteria in our research. The UNSDI-Transportation datamodel was applied for harmonization of the individual source datasets. 
 We have only included included highways, primary and secondary roads as part of this dataset. The original GRIP dataset consists of tertiary and local roads as well.

title: [Archived] Solar Irradiance
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](2063964b-56c8-4080-b2a5-5a7710f321b9) as a replacement.**_
  
Global Solar Atlas' solar irradiation dataset was developed by Solargis and provided by the World Bank Group. Solar resource, PV power potential, and air temperature data is aggregated long-term into yearly averages. The PV energy simulation is based on the use of re-computed and statistically aggregated 15-minute solar resource and air temperature data. This approach is consistent in terms of space and time, and it is provided as a quick assessment tool for exploration, site prospection and pre-feasibility analysis. The global horizontal irradiation (GHI) reflects the sum of direct and diffuse components of solar radiation.   
  
GHI is one of the principal climate phenomena that determines solar power generation and is considered a climate reference as it enables comparing individual sites or regions. Photovoltaic electricity output, or power potential, is the amount of energy, converted by a PV system into electricity (kWh/kWp) that is expected to be generated according to the geographical conditions of a site and a configuration of the PV system. Three configurations of a PV system are considered: (i) Small residential; (ii) Medium-size commercial; and (iii) Ground-mounted large scale.   
  
The data have a resolution of 1 km and spatial coverage between latitudes 60°N to 45°S. The data represent a time period from January 1994/1999/2007 until December 2015, depending on the satellite coverage. Presently, Solargis processes data from three satellite data providers (EUMETSAT, Japanese Meteorological Agency and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) with geostationary satellites operating at five key positions, to cover the entire world (except polar and subpolar regions). title: Aqueduct Riverine Flood Risk
description:
### Overview  
  
Riverine flood risk measures the percentage of the population expected to be affected by riverine flooding in an average year, accounting for existing flood-protection standards. Higher values indicate that a greater proportion of the population is expected to be impacted by riverine floods on average. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<0.1%) to extremely high (>1%).

  
  
Flood risk was assessed using hazard (inundation caused by river overflow), exposure (population in flood zone), and vulnerability. The existing level of flood protection was also incorporated into the risk calculation. It is important to note that this indicator represents flood risk not in terms of maximum possible impact but rather as average annual impact. The impacts from infrequent, extreme flood years were averaged with more common, less newsworthy flood years to produce the “expected annual affected population.”  Values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data on the population impacted by riverine floods were provided by Aqueduct Floods (Ward et al. forthcoming). Flood risk was simulated using a cascade of models within the Global Flood Risk with IMAGE Scenarios (GLOFRIS) modeling framework [(Winsemius et al. 2013)](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-17-1871-2013). Riverine hazard maps were derived using PCR-GLOBWB 2 inputs from 1960-1999. The riverine flood hazard is represented by inundation maps showing the flood extent and depth for floods of several return periods (2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, and 1000 years) at a horizontal resolution of 5’ x 5’ (regridded to 30” x 30”). Exposure is represented by gridded maps of 2010 population count per cell at a horizontal resolution of 30” x 30". Vulnerability is represented as a binary condition: people are either affected or they are not. Estimates of flood protection standards come from the [FLOPROS model](https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-16-1049-2016). 

  
  
The expected annual affected population was calculated using a risk curve [(Meyer et al. 2009)](https://doi.org/10.1897/IEAM_2008-031.1). To create the curve, the return periods were first converted into probabilities (i.e., 1/return period) and then plotted on the x-axis against the impacted population. Next, flood protection (return year converted to probability) was added to the graph as a vertical line. All impacts that fell to the right of the flood protection line (i.e., impacted by smaller floods) were assumed to be protected against floods and were removed from the calculation. The expected annual affected population was calculated by integrating the area under the curve to the left of the flood protection line.

  
  
The expected annual affected population was divided by total population to calculate the percent of the population expected to be affected annually by riverine floods.

  
  
Finally, raw riverine flood risk values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw riverine flood risk values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.

- Low (0-1): < 0 to 1 in 1,000 people
- Low to medium (1-2): 1 in 1,000 to 2 in 1,000 people
- Medium to high (2-3): 2 in 1,000 to 6 in 1,000 people
- High (3-4): 6 in 1,000 people to 1 in 100 people
- Extremely high (4-5): > 1 in 100 people

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

Urban Land Use (Areal) – Mexico
description:
### Overview  
  
The Urban Land Use (Areal) – Mexico dataset provides an estimation of land use land cover (LULC) for nine cities in Mexico. The nine cities are Culiacán, Guadalajara, León, Mérida, Mexico City, Monterrey, Reynosa, Tijuana, and Tuxtla Gutiérrez. Land cover indicates the physical cover over the surface of lands, such as water or vegetation, whereas land use shows how people use the land, such as commercial or plantation. A LULC map classifies areas within a set of categories. This dataset includes the following six categories: Open space, Nonresidential, Residential - Atomistic, Residential - Informal subdivision, Residential - Formal subdivision, and Residential - Housing project. (For full definitions of these categories, see [this working paper](https://marroninstitute.nyu.edu/uploads/content/Measuring_the_Quality_of_Urban_Layouts_December_1_2016_Reduced_new.pdf) or the [technical note](https://www.wri.org/publication/mapping-urban-land-use-in-india-and-mexico).) These "areal" categories exclude the major "linear" urban LULC category: Roads. The data is available for the year 2018 and has a resolution of 5 meters (m).
  
  

The dataset was produced by the World Resources Institute (WRI). It provides an insight into LULC within cities: what lies where and when. This information can play a critical role in urban planning and monitoring. The dataset can be used to measure the impact of different types of urban land use on air quality or identify what types of land use have been affected by natural disasters. Although this particular LULC dataset captures only one moment in time, when available there is also a high value to change detection over time, looking both forward, for planning purposes, and backward, to chart and understand the outcomes of past pressures, development, and policy decisions.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Urban Land Use (Areal) – Mexico dataset was produced in an automated way via supervised machine learning techniques. Automating urban LULC classification reduced the resource and time requirements by orders of magnitude, relative to manual mapping, thus making the process highly scalable. The machine learning model used for classification required two primary ingredients: satellite imagery and ground-truth data. Ground-truth is the observation or measurements about what actually exists at a specific location.This data was collected from the Atlas of Urban Expansion, a multiphase research effort conducted by the New York University (NYU) Urban Expansion Program in partnership with UN-Habitat and the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy. The Sentinel-2 constellation of the European Space Agency was used as the source of satellite imagery. The original resolution of the imagery was 10 m; this was later upsampled to 5 m to utilize as much information as possible from the ground-truth data.
  
  

The satellite imagery was combined with the ground-truth data to create training samples required for training the model. The models were relatively small, straightforward convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The trained models were finally used to map selected cities in Mexico. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/mapping-urban-land-use-in-india-and-mexico).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [roads](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e1c519d3-16ea-400a-a71c-9033ba5f490b) for the same nine cities in Mexico and LULC (areal) data for [India](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e354f7b8-0fca-422f-bf12-fc6189812bec).

title: Projected Annual Average Temperature U.S. (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps:

All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value.
All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value.
Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2.

The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: [Archived] Tree Cover

title: [Archived] Malaria Extent
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](3db2f914-2c70-431c-8dce-5dd961bccbd5) as a replacement.**_
  
The Malaria Extent data set is provided by the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) and shows the estimated proportion of 2-10 year olds in the general population that are infected with P. falciparum at any one time on the African continent, where the disease is endemic. Malaria is a disease caused by parasites that are transmitted to humans by Anopheles mosquitoes. Two related parasite species cause the majority of disease and death from malaria: Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. In areas affected by malaria, children and pregnant women are especially vulnerable, a condition further compounded by poverty. In Africa, where 80% of malaria cases are treated at home, the disease kills 1 child in 20 before the age of 5. MAP conducted surveys to collect data on malaria cases. Each survey included in the MAP parasite database has been disaggregated to individual sites (geographical points), individual dates (if the same site was sampled repeatedly), and individual parasite species. Conversely, individual-level survey data have been aggregated up to the community level at a particular site and time. MAP data spans 2000-2015. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset.
